messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Rhat for lp__
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Rhat for lp__
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, July 31, 2014 11:08:54 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Not for me!  I still want to know why the Rhats for lp__ are
> usually so much higher and whether it could be problematic for
> the parameter estimates if lp__ estimates don't seem to have
> converged according to Rhat.

Perhaps, but we already have examples where the Rhat is close to 1 for everything, including lp__, despite the chains not having converged.

To me, I think the bigger question is whether it makes sense to make a decision about a chain-level phenomenon (convergence) from the margins? A related question is that since the Markov Chain operates in the unconstrained space, does it make sense to evaluate convergence in the constrained space? The lp__ is at least a function of all the parameters, and it is the log-posterior with respect to the parameters in the unconstrained space. The Rhat makes more sense when you really care about one thing (which is presumably not lp__) and want to know how much is variance is inflated by having only a given number of draws.

Ben

> On Thursday, July 31, 2014 11:08:54 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> converged according to Rhat.
>
> Perhaps, but we already have examples where the Rhat is close to 1 for everything, including lp__, despite the chains not having converged.

I know that Rhat near 1 is necessary for convergence, but
not sufficient.

The question is really whether Rhat not having converged has
dire implications for the other parameters, which do have Rhat
near 1.

> To me, I think the bigger question is whether it makes sense to make a decision about a chain-level phenomenon (convergence) from the margins?

We can reject chain-level convergence of a vector
if one of the elements hasn't converged, right?

> A related question is that since the Markov Chain operates in the unconstrained space, does it make sense to evaluate convergence in the constrained space?

I don't see why not.  It's just a transform of the parameters.
Just like X^2 and I know that makes sense to monitor.

> The lp__ is at least a function of all the parameters, and it is the log-posterior with respect to the parameters in the unconstrained space.

Right.  Does that mean we should always run long enough that
Rhat for lp__ is close to 1?

> The Rhat makes more sense when you really care about one thing (which is presumably not lp__) and want to know how much is variance is inflated by having only a given number of draws.

I understand that, too.  We could invent all kinds of crazy functions
of parameters that wouldn't converge.  I'm just asking if lp__ is
one of them or whether its nonconvergence signals problems for the chain
as a whole.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Rhat for lp__
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Rhat for lp__
messages.body_plain:
1) Markov chain convergence is a global property and does not depend on the choice of function.
Rhat considers the composition of a Markov chain and a function, and if the Markov chain has
converged then each Markov chain + function composition will have converged.  Multivariate
functions converge when all of their margins have converged by the Cramer-Wold theorem.

2) The transformation from unconstrained space to constrained space is just another function,
so does not effect convergence.

3) Different functions may have different autocorrelations, but if the Markov chain has equilibrated
then all Markov chain + function compositions should be consistent with convergence.  Formally
any function that appears inconsistent is of concern and although it would be unreasonable to test
_every_ function, lp should at least be consistent.

The obvious difference in lp is that it tends to vary quickly with position and is consequently
susceptible to outliers.  Not to mention the fact that its magnitude is typically large and it’s worth
looking into how accurate the floating point computations are in the Rhat calculation.

messages.body_plain:
On Aug 1, 2014, at 11:55 AM, glae...@gmail.com wrote:

> Dear Stan Users,
>
> this is my first post and I just started in Stan (switching from JAGS), so please be patient with me ... :-)

We're very patient.

> My trial-by-trial (hierarchical) model processes two pieces of empirical data currently stored in R as:
> (1) M - a 3-dimensional matrix [3,nTrials,nSubjects]
> (2) FB - a 2-dimensional matrix [nSubjects,nTrials]
>
> In the model block I have 2 for-loops over subjects and trials. In the outer subjects-loop I need to access the then 2-dimensional matrix M, and the vector FB for that subject:
>
> After some deliberation on the Stan data types, I think it is most appropriate to declare M as an array of matrices and FB as an array of vectors, so that I can access them in the following way:
>
> data {
>   ...
>   matrix[128,3] M[337]; // 128 trials, 337 subjects
>   vector[128] FB[337];
>   vector[128] ONES[337]; // an array of vectors filled with 1's (for relating model predictions to the "virtual data" = all successes)

You should declare just a single vector[128] in transformed data,
fill it with ones using rep_vector(0,128), and then re-use it.

>   ...
> }
> model {
>
>   ... // declarations and sampling statements for hierarchical priors
>
>   for (sub in 1:nSubjects) {
>     matrix[128,3] m;
>     vector[128] fb;
>     vector[128] ones;
>
>     vector[128] prob;
>     matrix[128,3] a;

Stan is not BUGS.  You don't need to declare all these local variables
to use them.  This just incurs overhead in copying.

>     m <- M[s];
>     fb <- FB[s];
>     ones <- ONES[s];
>
>     ... // sample individual parameters from hierarchical priors
>
>     a[1,1] <- 1/3;
>     a[1,2] <- 1/3;
>     a[1,3] <- 1/3;

Why are you only setting a[1] and then using a[t]?  This will be a bug
because a[t] will be undefined for t > 1.

If you want each to be 1/3, then again, just declare a transformed
data variable and reuse it.

Again, Stan is not R.  Evaluating 1/3 yields 0.  Stan uses C++-style
arithmetic.  You need to use 1/3.0 or 1.0/3 or 1.0/3.0.  See the
manual for a discussion.  If you do it as above, the compiler will
give you a warning about trying to use division on integers.

>
>     for ( t in 1:nTrials) {
>       prob[t] <- dot_product(m[t],a[t]^d[sub]) / ( sum(a[t]^d[sub]) + machine_precision() ); // m = data, a = internal variable, d = model parameter

If you're going to use m[t], then just declare M
as a two-dimensional array of vectors and use
M[s,t] in this expression.  There is no copying involved
in just accessing an array.

I have no idea what you're trying to do by adding machine_precision to this.

>       ones[t] ~ bernoulli(prob[t]);

Again, you don't need to assign prob[t] to a local variable.  You can just
drop the expression inside as an argument.

Again, Stan is not R.  Stan variables are typed.  And bernoulli
requires integer arguments, not real arguments.  I think what you
really want to do is this:

  1 ~ bernoulli(prob[t]);

But it's probably better if you just vectorize and use

   1 ~ bernoulli(prob);

>       ... // update internal variables with feedback (fb) etc.
>     }
>   }
> }
>
> I have 5 questions:
> 1. Does the Stan data type (array of matrices/vectors) seem like an appropriate choice?

See above.

> 2. Would the declaration in the data block work, if a re-ordered by data in R to be M[nSubjects,nTrials,3] and FB[nSubjects,nTrials]?

As long as everything evaluates to the right type.

> 3. Do I have to pay attention to the vector orientation (row,column) in the dot_product(m[t],a[t]^d[sub]) expression?

No, but you might be able to simplify and speed things up by using
matrix arithmetic rather than repeated vector arithmetic and then
using a vectorized form of Bernoulli.

> 4. Is there are more elegant way to assign 1/3 to the first row of matrix a other than assigning each element as above)?

Yes, see above for why 1/3 won't work and what will work.

> 5. Is ones[t] ~ bernoulli(prob[t]) good programming in Stan (it worked in JAGS) or should I rather use increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(1,prob[t]))?

Neither.  Use 1 ~ bernoulli(prob); as described above.

-Bob

Other than in assignment statements, a <- b, expressions are
not sensitive to their form as long as they are the right type.

variable.

> > 2. Would the declaration in the data block work, if a re-ordered by data in R to be M[nSubjects,nTrials,3] and FB[nSubjects,nTrials]?

> Anyways, I am attaching the full model code with your suggestions already implemented (I think). If you have the time, I'd really appreciate if you took another look.

It must not compile and run yet, because it's "else if", not "elseif".

You don't want to declare a parameter with
constraint to lie in (0,1), as in:

  real<lower=0,upper=1> r_mu;

and then have a truncation that's narrower:

  r_mu ~ beta(A,B) T[L,U];

What you want to do is this:

  real<lower=L,upper=U> r_mu;

and then you only need

  r_mu ~ beta(A,B);

The truncation doesn't add anything to the log prob if L and
U are constants, and the constraint on r_mu makes sure the
model prob is non-zero for every value meeting the constraint.
Otherwise, if you had 0 < r_mu < L, you have a valid r_mu
for the constraint, but not in the model.

But you don't even need the sampling statement for r_mu,
because A = 1 and B = 1, so r_mu gets a uniform prior, which
is the default if you don't add anything in the model.  Stan
is smart enough to just not do anything with the r_mu sampling
statement though other than error checking, so it won't be
a noticeable overhead.

Also, Stan tends to be more stable than JAGS or BUGS, so
you usually don't need to do things like .001 lower bounds
and .999 upper bounds.

Also, you can assign A <- 1 no problem.  Integers will be promoted
to reals where required.  It's just in the 1/3 case that nothing
is causing them to be promoted, so it's integer arithmetic.

As to putting assignments in the transformed parameters or as local
variables in the model is just a matter of whether they get saved
as parameters in the output.

- Bob

> I'm not sure what you mean with "random effects for diameter and length". Previously, you had fixed effects for diameter and length. Did you change your model? Just in case: in your posterior predictive checks, you shouldn't resample the coefficients for diameter and length. If you do (and also resample the sigma's), you step into the arena of prior predictive checks (which I've never used before, but there's plenty of literature on it if you want to find out what it's for).
>
> What do you mean by decent in "SSQ of Pearson residuals or just SSQ for new batches don't provide decent  p-value (not equal 0 or 1)"? You want your p-value to be far away from 0 and 1, right? Next, you could use an information criterion to compare models with and without the overdispersion parameter (the WAIC has been suggested before elsewhere on this list). You might even be able to do some sort posterior predictive check with a clever discrepancy test to see whether the overdispersion makes sense (although I would have to think longer about that, have to run now).

messages.body_plain:
Hi Linus,

Nice clean code, easy to read :).

First of all, you might want to check how reasonable the assumption is that the three random effects are not correlated. In the model section, your code says:

intercept ~ normal (0, 1);
	d ~ normal (0, 1);
	l ~ normal (0, 1);

If in fact these random effects are correlated (check by scattering the draws from the posterior against each other) - which they probably are - you get into trouble when you generate replicate data based on resampled random effects. In other words, in your mixed prior/posterior predictive checks, your resampled random effects are assumed to be independent, whereas they probably are not. Therefore, I recommend that you model the three normalized random effects through a multivariate normal. See elsewhere on this list for advice about efficiently sampling from multivariate normal distributions.

Second, I strongly recommend that you plot data and replicate data on the log-scale (the first two figures; not necessary for residuals). It's hard to see what's happening near the origin. Also, add an identity line (y = x) to each of the scatter plots. Otherwise it's hard to see what's happening, especially in the graphs *SSQ.jpg (you might want to make the scales and ranges the same for the y and x axes).

I'm not sure that "ExistingLots.jpg" is showing what it's supposed to. What do the axes represent? If it's replicated data (pred_counts) versus observed data, it should look similar in shape to "NewLots.jpg", but with the means approximately lined up along the line y=x. I would also expect to see at least some variation (error bars) due to the random Poisson samples.

I presume that in the *SSQ.jpg figures, each open circle represents a draw from the posterior? To interpret these figures, you need the line y=x and equal scale and ranges for the axes. Judging from the p-values (0.93 for new lots), something funny is going on. This could be due to the independent sampling of random effects, so you should first fix that (see above). After having done so, (and regardless of whether it solves the issue,) you might want to produce sums of squared residuals per lot and calculate p-values for those to see whether any of lots are deviating from the general pattern.

Regarding checking the means and sd's, I'm not sure I understand what you are trying to do. What did you calculate means and sd's for? Are the histograms the posterior? Of what? Is the red line the mean or sd of the data?

Best,

Luc

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Rhat for lp__
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Rhat for lp__
messages.body_plain:
Issue One: What is Convergence?

There is no hard cutoff between “transience” and “equilibrium".  What happens is that as N-> infinity the distribution of possible states in the Markov chain approaches the target distribution and _in that limit_ the expected value of the Monte Carlo estimator of _any integrable function_ converges to the true expectation.  There is nothing like warmup here because in the N->infinity limit the effects of initial state are completely washed out.

The problem is what happens for finite N.  If we can prove a strong _geometric ergodicity_ property (which depends on the sampler and the target distribution) then one can show that there exists a finite time after which the chain forgets its initial state with a large probability.  This is both the autocorrelation time and the warmup time — but even if you can show it exists and is finite (which is nigh impossible) you can’t compute an actual value analytically.

So what you do in practice is hope that N is large enough for the expectations to be reasonably accurate.  Removing warmup iterations improves the accuracy of the expectations but there is no guarantee that removing any finite number of samples will be enough.

Issue Two: Why Inconsistent Rhats?

There are two things to worry about here.

Firstly, as noted above, for any finite N there will always be some residual effect of the initial state, which typically manifests as some small (or large if the autocorrelation time is huge) probability of having a large outlier.  Functions robust to such outliers (say, quantiles) will appear more stable and have better Rhats.  Functions vulnerable to such outliers may show fragility.

Secondly, Rhat makes very strong assumptions.  In particular is assumes that the functions being considered are Gaussian (or it only uses the first two moments and assumes some kind of independence — the point is that strong assumptions are made) that do not always hold.  In particular, the distribution for the log posterior density almost never looks Gaussian, instead it features long tails that can lead to large Rhats even in the large N limit.

The tweaks that Andrew keeps talking about all have the flavor of making the samples of interest more Gaussian and hence the Rhat calculation more accurate.

Conclusion:

“Convergence” is a global property and holds for all integrable functions at once, but Rhat requires additional assumptions so may not work for all functions equally well.

Note that if you just compare the _expectations_ between chains then we can rely on the Markov chain asymptotics for Gaussian distributions and can apply the standard tests.

is:

derivative tests for all our functions take days to run because

implementations branch on all these.

patch is merged.

>>>> We can reject chain-level convergence of a vector
>>>> if one of the elements hasn't converged, right?
>>>>
>>>>> A related question is that since the Markov Chain operates in the unconstrained space, does it make sense to evaluate convergence in the constrained space?
>>>>
>>>> I don't see why not.  It's just a transform of the parameters.
>>>> Just like X^2 and I know that makes sense to monitor.
>>>>
>>>>> The lp__ is at least a function of all the parameters, and it is the log-posterior with respect to the parameters in the unconstrained space.
>>>>
>>>> Right.  Does that mean we should always run long enough that
>>>> Rhat for lp__ is close to 1?
>>>>
>>>>> The Rhat makes more sense when you really care about one thing (which is presumably not lp__) and want to know how much is variance is inflated by having only a given number of draws.
>>>>
>>>> I understand that, too.  We could invent all kinds of crazy functions
>>>> of parameters that wouldn't converge.  I'm just asking if lp__ is
>>>> one of them or whether its nonconvergence signals problems for the chain
>>>> as a whole.

messages.body_plain:
Stan's compiler doesn't build *under Windows* without optimization.
The problem with -O0 is that the debug info being generated blows
out the memory of their rather lame C++ toolchain.  We've had to
implement several painful workarounds even to get the optimized
versions to compile under Windows.

None of the dev team uses Windows for development, so we use it
for our integration server just to make sure it's getting tested.
We're going to add continuous integration for Linux and Mac OS soon,
though it's never caused us a problem --- basically if something
can be made to work on Windows, it has worked everywhere else.

Everyone uses different debugging tactics.  I'm still a fan of
debug-by-printf.  I almost always find it easier than using
a step-through debugger.  I do find debuggers really useful to
get a feel for the call chain in code I'm not familiar with.
I believe others use gdb, Xcode, and various memory profiling
tools for leaks.  I think most of our profiling has been in Xcode,
though that's just because I don't know what the linux users use.

- Bob

On 8/1/2014 7:13 PM, Luc Coffeng wrote:

> Hi Linus,
>
> Nice clean code, easy to read :).
>
> First of all, you might want to check how reasonable the assumption is that the three random effects are not correlated. In the model section, your code says:
>
> intercept ~ normal (0, 1);
> 	d ~ normal (0, 1);
> 	l ~ normal (0, 1);
>
> If in fact these random effects are correlated (check by scattering the draws from the posterior against each other) - which they probably are - you get into trouble when you generate replicate data based on resampled random effects. In other words, in your mixed prior/posterior predictive checks, your resampled random effects are assumed to be independent, whereas they probably are not. Therefore, I recommend that you model the three normalized random effects through a multivariate normal. See elsewhere on this list for advice about efficiently sampling from multivariate normal distributions.
>
> Second, I strongly recommend that you plot data and replicate data on the log-scale (the first two figures; not necessary for residuals). It's hard to see what's happening near the origin. Also, add an identity line (y = x) to each of the scatter plots. Otherwise it's hard to see what's happening, especially in the graphs *SSQ.jpg (you might want to make the scales and ranges the same for the y and x axes).
>
> I'm not sure that "ExistingLots.jpg" is showing what it's supposed to. What do the axes represent? If it's replicated data (pred_counts) versus observed data, it should look similar in shape to "NewLots.jpg", but with the means approximately lined up along the line y=x. I would also expect to see at least some variation (error bars) due to the random Poisson samples.
>
> I presume that in the *SSQ.jpg figures, each open circle represents a draw from the posterior? To interpret these figures, you need the line y=x and equal scale and ranges for the axes. Judging from the p-values (0.93 for new lots), something funny is going on. This could be due to the independent sampling of random effects, so you should first fix that (see above). After having done so, (and regardless of whether it solves the issue,) you might want to produce sums of squared residuals per lot and calculate p-values for those to see whether any of lots are deviating from the general pattern.
>
> Regarding checking the means and sd's, I'm not sure I understand what you are trying to do. What did you calculate means and sd's for? Are the histograms the posterior? Of what? Is the red line the mean or sd of the data?
>
> Best,
>
> Luc

messages.subject: OpenMx and Stan
messages.subject_clean: OpenMx and Stan
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Aug 02, 2014 at 12:28:22PM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > In OpenMx, multi_normal has two implementations. One implementation
> > handles data in the form of 1 case per row. The other implementation
> > handles data as a covariance matrix (and means). These two approaches
> > are equivalent for certain data (no missingness, etc).
>
> We don't have the latter in Stan, but now that you mention it,
> it seems like a good idea.  Should be much faster to compute the
> stats on the data and then make a single call.

Yes, of course

If you're interested in further bridging the gap between Stan and
OpenMx, the next important feature would be RAM. Most OpenMx users don't
specify a model expected covariance matrix directly. Most OpenMx users
use the RAM specification (McArdle & McDonald, 1984).

In RAM, the covariance matrix is specified using an A and S matrix. The
A matrix gives the directional predictors (regressions) and the S matrix
gives the covariances. The benefit of this parameterization is that it
has a nice intuitive graphical interpretation. Some of my colleagues
developed a graphical, introductory SEM program,

  http://onyx.brandmaier.de/

I'm not sure if Stan needs anything special to support RAM. The RAM
model expected covariance and mean vector are given by

\Sigma = F(I-A)^{-1} S(I-A)^T F^T
\mu = F(I-A)^{-1} m

where F is a filter matrix to select the manifest variables (hiding the
latent variables).

Can Stan already produce efficient derivatives for these expressions?

Since there are usually not long chains of regressions, there is a trick
to invert (I-A) very efficiently.

If this is easily accommodated in Stan then it would be a small step to
add "Export to Stan" functions in both Onyx and OpenMx. The vast
majority of SEM models are essentially multivariate Normal RAM models
(using either sufficient statistics or full information).

--
Joshua N. Pritikin
Department of Psychology
University of Virginia
485 McCormick Rd, Gilmer Hall Room 102
Charlottesville, VA 22904
http://people.virginia.edu/~jnp3bc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Linas,

It looks like you did things right. In the full posterior predictive checks, it seems that poisson sampling error is relatively small compared to the marginal variance of the data, hence the "smooth" line in "ExistingLots.jpg". If you'd zoom in enough, you'd probably see the Poisson sampling error. But like I said, using full posterior predictive checks for a hierarchical model overestimates the model's predictive validity.

I seems that modeling the correlation of random effects did improve the predictive validity of the model, as the Bayesian p-value for the mixed PPC changed from 0.93 to 0.80, which would make me feel much more comfortable making predictions. Just curious: what were the correlations of the random effects?

To even better understand the model and the data, you may still want to evaluate the SSQ within each lot. Probably, one or a few lots are responsible for the results you see in NewLotsSSQ.jpg. My guess would be that the lot in the left bottom corner of NewLots.jpg is contributing considerably to the total SSQ.

Good luck finishing up!

Luc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luc:

Thank you for your recommendations and the vectorized version of the model. Vectorizing the STAN code and moving 'rho' to the generated quantities block reduced the total warm-up and sampling time from ~4.5 minutes to ~2 minutes (for each chain, ~45 seconds for warmup and ~15 seconds for sampling). It takes about 20 seconds to compile the model. The vast majority of the warm-up time is spent on the first 100 iterations in which the inverse wishart prior does appear to produce covariance matrices that are not positive definite; once resolved, estimation speeds up dramatically. Again, thank you for your clear and thorough assistance!

If I may, I do have a couple of follow-up questions about the model compilation. For the simulation study, the sample size from one replication to the next will not constant. Rather, in order to not capitalize on the whims of a specific sample size, I specify a small range of sample sizes when generating data to allow sample sizes to differ between replications. So my questions are the following... Does the compilation of the model depend on the particular sample size? If not, after compiling the model for the first replication, how does one avoid the compilation step for subsequent replications?

Cheers,

Derek

On Sunday, August 3, 2014 12:33:30 AM UTC-7, Luc Coffeng wrote:
> Hi Derek,
>
> You will want to compare number of effective samples per second or seconds per effective sample, rather than total running time. Also, if you are repeatedly fitting the same model to different datasets, you only have to compile the stan model once.
>
> You can improve the speed of the stan model by vectorizing the sampling statements. See below; I vectorized things over N, assuming that N>J. If J>N, it would be more efficient to vectorize over J. See below for the vectorized code.
>
> Note that univariate normal distributions in Stan are defined with standard deviation, not variance.
>
> You can move things that are not used in the model to the generated quantities block (rho in this case), so they aren't recalculated for every leapfrog step (everything in the parameters, transformed parameters, and the model blocks is executed/calculated for every leapfrog step in the discrete HMC simulation).
>
> Last, there are a few people around here that like to stay away from gamma and inverse wishart priors (I'll leave it to them to explain it, they'll do a much better job at it). For the bivariate normal case, you're probably better off modeling standard errors and correlation as separate parameters.
>
> Best,
>
> Luc
>
> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> data {
>   int<lower=0> N;           // Number of subjects.
>   int<lower=0> J;           // Number of measurement occasions.
>   vector[N] y[J];           // Dimensions of the observed data.
>   vector[J] time;           // Balanced coding of time (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2)
>   cov_matrix[2] Omega;      // Diagonal matrix on growth params (prior).
> }
>
> parameters {
>   vector[2] beta[N];        // level-1 growth parameters.
>   vector[2] gamma;          // level-2 intercept and linear parameters.
>   real gamma20;             // level-2 quadratic parameter.
>   real<lower=.001> ressd;   // homoskedastics residual variance
>   cov_matrix[2] psi;        // covariance matrix among growth parameters.
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>   real ressd;               // standard deviation of residuals
>   ressd <- sqrt(resvar);
> }
>
> model {
>   vector[N] mu[J];           // temporary variable for expected values
>
>   resvar ~ inv_gamma(.001,.001);   // residual variance prior.
>   gamma ~ normal(0,1000);          // diffuse prior on intercept and linear growth params.
>   gamma20 ~ normal(0,1000);        // diffuse prior on quadratic growth param
>   psi ~ inv_wishart(2,Omega);      // prior on intercept and linear covariance matrix
>   beta ~ multi_normal(gamma,psi);  // prior on level-1 intercept and linear growth params.
>
>
>   for(j in 1:J) {
>     for(i in 1:N) {
>       mu[j,i] <- beta[i,1] + beta[i,2] * time[j] + gamma20 * (time[j] * time[j]);
>     }
>     y[j] ~ normal(mu[j], ressd);  // growth model. ***
>   }
> }
>
> generated quantities {
>   // real rho;
>   // rho <- psi[1,2] / sqrt(psi[1,1] * psi[2,2]);
> }
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] OpenMx and Stan
messages.body_plain:
On Aug 2, 2014, at 10:20 PM, Joshua N Pritikin <jpri...@pobox.com> wrote:

> On Sat, Aug 02, 2014 at 12:28:22PM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>> In OpenMx, multi_normal has two implementations. One implementation
>>> handles data in the form of 1 case per row. The other implementation
>>> handles data as a covariance matrix (and means). These two approaches
>>> are equivalent for certain data (no missingness, etc).
>>
>> We don't have the latter in Stan, but now that you mention it,
>> it seems like a good idea.  Should be much faster to compute the
>> stats on the data and then make a single call.
>
> Yes, of course
>
> If you're interested in further bridging the gap between Stan and
> OpenMx, the next important feature would be RAM. Most OpenMx users don't
> specify a model expected covariance matrix directly. Most OpenMx users
> use the RAM specification (McArdle & McDonald, 1984).
>
> In RAM, the covariance matrix is specified using an A and S matrix. The
> A matrix gives the directional predictors (regressions) and the S matrix
> gives the covariances. The benefit of this parameterization is that it
> has a nice intuitive graphical interpretation. Some of my colleagues
> developed a graphical, introductory SEM program,
>
>  http://onyx.brandmaier.de/
>
> I'm not sure if Stan needs anything special to support RAM. The RAM
> model expected covariance and mean vector are given by
>
> \Sigma = F(I-A)^{-1} S(I-A)^T F^T
> \mu = F(I-A)^{-1} m
>
> where F is a filter matrix to select the manifest variables (hiding the
> latent variables).
>
> Can Stan already produce efficient derivatives for these expressions?

I'm assuming T is transpose.

The trick in getting efficient and numerically stable expressions is
to avoid inverse.  So rather than directly evaluating F * (I - A)^{-1},
you'd evaluate F / (I - A), where matrix division is defined by

   (X / Y) =def= X * Y^{-1}.

And yes, we can do these relatively efficiently.   It'd be more efficient to
build in derivatives for the whole expression, but autodiffing with the
above shouldn't be a problem.

> Since there are usually not long chains of regressions, there is a trick
> to invert (I-A) very efficiently.

See above.

But if there's something more efficient we can do because I is known to
be an identity matrix, then we don't have that built in.  Do you have
references on the trick required?

>
> If this is easily accommodated in Stan then it would be a small step to
> add "Export to Stan" functions in both Onyx and OpenMx. The vast
> majority of SEM models are essentially multivariate Normal RAM models
> (using either sufficient statistics or full information).
>

I don't even know what a "SEM model" is, but I assume other people
do.  I saw some description of structural equation modeling in Sophia
Rabe-Hesketh's book on hierarchical models, but I didn't really
understand the notation, though it seemed to be underlyingly a notation
for regression.

- Bob

>

On Aug 3, 2014, at 12:21 PM, Hang Zeng <caff...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Stan developers,
>
> The code is running wrong when I do a simple log-normal model. Can you help me to have a look? Thank you.
> My computer system is windows 8.1 and running Stan (2.2.0) on R x64 3.1.0. Here is my simple Rstan model, initial values and warning.
> If you wanna the data to check where wrong is, I will send to you in privacy. Thank you so much again.
>
> Rstan model:
> data {
>     int<lower=0> n;
>     real y[n];
> }
>
> parameters {
>
>   real<lower=0> sigma;
>
>   real mu;
> }
>
> model {
>
>  y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
> }

The above can't be the model that produced the message below.

In the model block, the variable n will only use the very last
value, which isn't enough to pin down sigma.  What you want to do is:

for (i in 1:n)
   y[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma);

or better yet, just vectorize and write this:

   y ~ normal(mu,sigma);

This isn't a lognormal model, by the way.

- Bob

> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,

Hi Derek,

Glad to help and rewarding to see that the total running time was more than halved.

You don't have to recompile the model as long as the structure is exactly the same. The exact dimenions of vectors and matrices don't have to be the same (though they should probably be at least >1), as long as you haven't hardcoded these somewhere outside the data block.

Just to reiterate: when you have to choose between JAGS and Stan, compare in terms of seconds per effective sample size, not total running time. In the end, you will only need a certain effective sample size. I don't have any recommendations on that (I like being on the safe side and use brute force, but that's not really an appealing option for your simulation study). Some of the Stan Developers may be able to advise on the minimal number of effective samples.

Regarding the Metropolis rejections of the covariance matrices, you can probably gain significant efficiency by modeling it differently. There are several good alternatives in Stan, including modeling the correlation matrix with an LKJ prior, and scaling it with a vector of sigmas (sigma ~ cauchy(0,5) is usually a safe bet, adjust scale to expectation). Alternatively, you could model the sigmas and rho separely (rho ~ uniform(-1,1); this works in JAGS too). You can check the manual for other parameterizations of the multivariate normal. In general, you want to avoid using the "normal" multivariate normal as its evaluation involves computationally expensive matrix inversions (especially for >=trivariate cases) that can be numerically unstable and lead to Metropolis rejections.

Good luck,

Luc

On Aug 3, 2014, at 12:45 PM, Derek Fay <derek.f...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Luc:
>
> Thank you for your recommendations and the vectorized version of the model. Vectorizing the STAN code and moving 'rho' to the generated quantities block reduced the total warm-up and sampling time from ~4.5 minutes to ~2 minutes (for each chain, ~45 seconds for warmup and ~15 seconds for sampling). It takes about 20 seconds to compile the model. The vast majority of the warm-up time is spent on the first 100 iterations in which the inverse wishart prior does appear to produce covariance matrices that are not positive definite; once resolved, estimation speeds up dramatically. Again, thank you for your clear and thorough assistance!

We recommend other priors --- the inverse wishart is only popular
because it's conjugate so used in BUGS/JAGS, which as far as I know
only handle conjugate priors for multivariate quantities.

Having said that, the reason things are slow during warmup is that
Stan is adapting to the scales of each variable for sampling.

The positive-definiteness failures during warmup are usually due to
too large a step size, which will get corrected if warmup converges
to sensible adaptation parameters for step size and diagonal mass
matrix (basically, scale of each variable).

> If I may, I do have a couple of follow-up questions about the model compilation. For the simulation study, the sample size from one replication to the next will not constant. Rather, in order to not capitalize on the whims of a specific sample size, I specify a small range of sample sizes when generating data to allow sample sizes to differ between replications. So my questions are the following... Does the compilation of the model depend on the particular sample size?

Not if it's specified as data.  The only time you need to recompile
is when the model changes in the literal sense of being different text.

> If not, after compiling the model for the first replication, how does one avoid the compilation step for subsequent replications?

That depends on whether you are using CmdStan, RStan or PyStan.

Some more comments on the model below.

- Bob

> Cheers,
>
> Derek
>
> On Sunday, August 3, 2014 12:33:30 AM UTC-7, Luc Coffeng wrote:
> Hi Derek,
>
> You will want to compare number of effective samples per second or seconds per effective sample, rather than total running time. Also, if you are repeatedly fitting the same model to different datasets, you only have to compile the stan model once.
>
> You can improve the speed of the stan model by vectorizing the sampling statements. See below; I vectorized things over N, assuming that N>J. If J>N, it would be more efficient to vectorize over J. See below for the vectorized code.
>
> Note that univariate normal distributions in Stan are defined with standard deviation, not variance.
>
> You can move things that are not used in the model to the generated quantities block (rho in this case), so they aren't recalculated for every leapfrog step (everything in the parameters, transformed parameters, and the model blocks is executed/calculated for every leapfrog step in the discrete HMC simulation).
>
> Last, there are a few people around here that like to stay away from gamma and inverse wishart priors (I'll leave it to them to explain it, they'll do a much better job at it). For the bivariate normal case, you're probably better off modeling standard errors and correlation as separate parameters.
>
> Best,
>
> Luc
>
> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> data {
>   int<lower=0> N;           // Number of subjects.
>   int<lower=0> J;           // Number of measurement occasions.
>   vector[N] y[J];           // Dimensions of the observed data.
>   vector[J] time;           // Balanced coding of time (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2)
>   cov_matrix[2] Omega;      // Diagonal matrix on growth params (prior).
> }
>
> parameters {
>   vector[2] beta[N];        // level-1 growth parameters.
>   vector[2] gamma;          // level-2 intercept and linear parameters.
>   real gamma20;             // level-2 quadratic parameter.
>   real<lower=.001> ressd;   // homoskedastics residual variance
>   cov_matrix[2] psi;        // covariance matrix among growth parameters.
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>   real ressd;               // standard deviation of residuals
>   ressd <- sqrt(resvar);
> }
>

you can define ressd as a local variable in the model if you don't
need to save it and it'll cut down on a bit of I/O.

> model {
>   vector[N] mu[J];           // temporary variable for expected values
>
>   resvar ~ inv_gamma(.001,.001);   // residual variance prior.

These priors can be bad news.  I know it was standard practice in
earlier versions of BUGS, but even they are not recommending these
priors any more.  We'd recommend using something like a half-cauchy,
as in:

  resvar ~ cauchy(0,5);

or even a tighter prior depending on what you know about resvar ahead of time.

>   gamma ~ normal(0,1000);          // diffuse prior on intercept and linear growth params.
>   gamma20 ~ normal(0,1000);        // diffuse prior on quadratic growth param

It's more efficient in some cases to take these as normal(0,1) and
then scale gamma and gamma20 by 1000.  But adaptation can usually sort
out the scales with a bit of work (the time warmup's taking).

>   psi ~ inv_wishart(2,Omega);      // prior on intercept and linear covariance matrix
>   beta ~ multi_normal(gamma,psi);  // prior on level-1 intercept and linear growth params.
>
>
>   for(j in 1:J) {
>     for(i in 1:N) {
>       mu[j,i] <- beta[i,1] + beta[i,2] * time[j] + gamma20 * (time[j] * time[j]);
>     }
>     y[j] ~ normal(mu[j], ressd);  // growth model. ***

You could go even further vectorizing this given that ressd is shared,
and put all of the variables in one big array.  Probably won't make a difference
if N is large.

>   }
> }
>
> generated quantities {
>   // real rho;
>   // rho <- psi[1,2] / sqrt(psi[1,1] * psi[2,2]);
> }

If you only use a two by two covariance matrix, then it will be much
more efficient to parameterize the model in terms of a correlation
parameter rho between -1 and 1 and two positive scale parameters,
sqrt(psi[1,1]) and sqrt(psi[2,2]).   Then you can put the 2 x 2 covariance
matrix together directly.

The downside is that this only works for the 2 by 2 case.

It's even more efficient to parameterize in terms of cholesky factors,
but I'll stop here.  The next version of the manual's going to have
a lot more advice on priors from both a statistical and efficiency
perspective.

- Bob

Let me re-emphasize what Luc says --- only the number of effective
samples per second matters when comparing speed as that determines
the MCMC error (the MCMC version of std error) in your estimates of
posterior means (or other expectations over the posterior).

You've also chosen a particularly easy model for JAGS due to
the use of conjugate priors.  Gibbs can be very efficient when everything
is conjugate and there's not too much correlation among parameters in
the posterior.  We're not claiming to be faster than JAGS for every conceivable
model.

If Stan converges in fewer iterations, it should also have a higher n_eff
per iteration (i.e., it should mix faster), so you should see a
different story when measuring effective samples rather than iterations.

- Bob

The key words in that error message is "If this warning occurs sporadically…". While Drs. Gelman, Goodrich, and Betancourt can explain this much more rigorously, sometimes, the sampler picks a value that is illegal when it "jumps" around. If this is infrequent, it isn't a big deal. If it is constant, you may want to think about re-parameterizing the model.

Avi

On Thu, Jul 24, 2014 at 12:49 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Do you get warnings printed out as you go about failures
> in the covariance matrix tests?
>
> I'm hoping the problem is that our covariance matrix and
> correlation matrix consistency checks are too stringent and
> causing unnecessary failures.  That's been the case before.
>
> The underlying problem with more variables is that floating
> point arithmetic just isn't that precise, and when you have
> lots of operations (as in Cholesky factor multiplication
> and solvers converting the constrained/unconstrained), the
> results vary from what you'd get from infinite-precision
> arithmetic in that we can lose symmetry or positive definiteness.
>
> Another problem is if estimates get pushed up against boundaries
> (here correlation = 1 or -1, sd = 0 or +infinity).  This is
> also very unstable arithmetically.
>
> You might want to try again with Stan 2.4 --- we tried to clean
> some of these things up, but we probably still have a ways to go.
>
> - Bob
>
>

On Sun, Aug 03, 2014 at 12:58:11PM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On Aug 2, 2014, at 10:20 PM, Joshua N Pritikin <jpri...@pobox.com> wrote:
> > I'm not sure if Stan needs anything special to support RAM. The RAM
> > model expected covariance and mean vector are given by
> >
> > \Sigma = F(I-A)^{-1} S(I-A)^T F^T
> > \mu = F(I-A)^{-1} m
> >
> > where F is a filter matrix to select the manifest variables (hiding the
> > latent variables).
> >
> > Can Stan already produce efficient derivatives for these expressions?
>
> I'm assuming T is transpose.

Yes

> The trick in getting efficient and numerically stable expressions is
> to avoid inverse.  So rather than directly evaluating F * (I - A)^{-1},
> you'd evaluate F / (I - A), where matrix division is defined by
>
>    (X / Y) =def= X * Y^{-1}.
>
> And yes, we can do these relatively efficiently.   It'd be more efficient to
> build in derivatives for the whole expression, but autodiffing with the
> above shouldn't be a problem.

OK, there is a paper on computing derivatives for this model,

http://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13428-013-0384-4

But it would be nice to have anything working and then worry about
efficiency later.

> > Since there are usually not long chains of regressions, there is a trick
> > to invert (I-A) very efficiently.
>
> See above.
>
> But if there's something more efficient we can do because I is known to
> be an identity matrix, then we don't have that built in.  Do you have
> references on the trick required?

The idea is to find out how many terms of the Taylor expansion you need
for an exact solution.

To find out how many terms you need, you multiply A by itself until all
coefficents are zero. This usually happens within a few iterations
because RAM models rarely have regression loops. Then the Taylor
expansion is

         (I + A)
     I + (I + A) * A
I + (I + (I + A) * A) * A
 etc.

Of course it is better to have working code first and optimize it later.

> > If this is easily accommodated in Stan then it would be a small step to
> > add "Export to Stan" functions in both Onyx and OpenMx. The vast
> > majority of SEM models are essentially multivariate Normal RAM models
> > (using either sufficient statistics or full information).
>
> I don't even know what a "SEM model" is, but I assume other people
> do.  I saw some description of structural equation modeling in Sophia
> Rabe-Hesketh's book on hierarchical models, but I didn't really
> understand the notation, though it seemed to be underlyingly a notation
> for regression.

I agree that the terminology can be a barrier. SEM usually means
multivariate Normal. There are two popular parameterizations of the
multivariate Normal, RAM and LISREL. In Stan, you have embraced so many
diverse distributions, it may be difficult to imagine that an entire
academic field is devoted to just one of them.

--
Joshua N. Pritikin
Department of Psychology
University of Virginia
485 McCormick Rd, Gilmer Hall Room 102
Charlottesville, VA 22904
http://people.virginia.edu/~jnp3bc

Hi folks,

I have a quick question: is there a way to easily count the number of function (and/or gradient) evaluations in a particular run?
For example, I would like to see how many calls to the probability density function for particular numbers of iterations.
A Rstan solution is preferred, but any of the flavors work.

The hackish way would be to implement the function oneself, but it's a bit more tedious than I like.

Thanks!

Marshall

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Easy way to count function/gradient evaluations
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Easy way to count function/gradient evaluations
messages.body_plain:
There's no way to recover the exact number of evaluations
because some of them are eliminated due to the way the
NUTS algorithm achieves detailed balance.  The number
of kept evaluations is 2^treedepth per iteration.  As many
as 2^depth might also be discarded per iteration, but that's
relatively rare.

So it'd be sum(2^treedepth) for a lower bound on the number
of such evaluations.  I'm not sure how to recover that from
RStan offhand, but it's in the doc.

You can always dump a print statement in, which will print
every evaluation, then count those, if you just want to know
for some particular situation.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The problem is that our probably functions drop all the constant
terms in sampling statements

 x ~ distribution(...);

so you're not  getting the entire log probability function.
If you replace the sampling statements with

  increment_log_prob(distribution_log(x, ...));

that will not drop the constant terms.

- Bob

Thanks for finding and linking.

To summarize the thread and answer my own question:

1.  Michael's point was that you can't compute the relevant
integral for the marginal probability of the data
using MCMC because it has infinite variance.

2.  Andrew's point was that these factors don't make
much sense with very broad priors, and that if you want
to compare models, cross-validation or WAIC are better
(though still imperfect) tools.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Calculating Bayes Factor with Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

I don't know whether this has been discussed earlier, but there are methods
to calculate the marginal likelihood from the output of MCMC.

See the work by Chib https://stat.duke.edu/~scs/Courses/Stat376/Papers/NormConstants/ChibJASA1995.pdf
He uses the output from Gibbs to calculate the marginal likelihood. However, you need to do some additional
sampling that you wouldn't normally do,  to be able to calculate the marginal likelihood.

I've personally used his method to calculate the normalising constant of a particular generalisation
of a multivariate von mises distribution.

Regards,
Sachintha.

Hi.

I used Rstan 2.3 without problems: I suppressed the output by using refresh=-1 in my loops (I'm doing 5000 replications for 2 models, I really don't want the output of all).
But since I updated (upgraded?) to 2.4, I get the output, regardless of refresh=-1.

Same area, different issue: If I want a refresh every, say, 100 iteraties, I now get a new line for each one, where before it would just update the last refresh.
So now I get:
SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'ar_stan1' NOW (CHAIN 3).

Iteration:    1 / 2000 [  0%]  (Warmup)
Iteration:  100 / 2000 [  5%]  (Warmup)
Iteration:  200 / 2000 [ 10%]  (Warmup)
Iteration:  300 / 2000 [ 15%]  (Warmup)
Iteration:  400 / 2000 [ 20%]  (Warmup)

In stead of:
SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'ar_stan1' NOW (CHAIN 3).
Iteration:  400 / 2000 [ 20%]  (Warmup)

I also update R to 3.1.1, I had 3.0.2.

So, my questions are:
1. Can I get Rstan to not give ANY output if there is no error, as formerly with refresh=-1?
2. Can I get Rstan to update the refresh line in stead of give me a new one every time?

I hear about the sink() option, and will try it if the answer to the above is no. However, I work with several models at once, soms frequentistic, so I would like to be able to see messages from other models.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Integer floor calculation or type casting
messages.body_plain:
Hello again,

Sorry to bump this old thread, but it seems most relevant to a new question I have:

I am trying to take the mean value of an integer array (basically finding the expectation value of a binary vector) and am not sure how to do it.  When simply using the mean function, the parser throws the error:

no matches for function name="mean"
    arg 0 type=int[1]
available function signatures for mean:
0.  mean(real[1]) : real
1.  mean(vector) : real
2.  mean(row vector) : real
3.  mean(matrix) : real
no matches for function name="mean"
    arg 0 type=int[1]
available function signatures for mean:
0.  mean(real[1]) : real
1.  mean(vector) : real
2.  mean(row vector) : real
3.  mean(matrix) : real
expression is ill formed

This seems to be another type casting issue.  The manual states "Stan automatically promotes integer values to real values if necessary," but this does not seem to hold in this case.

One approach I have considered is to calculate the mean manually, by summing the integers and dividing by the vector length, but I think that will lead to integer rather than float division.

This was meant to go in the transformed data block of my model, so for now I can just precompute the mean and pass it as data.  But perhaps there is a better way to do this directly in Stan.

Thanks for any advice!

Best,

~Nathan

On Friday, November 8, 2013 2:13:31 PM UTC-5, Marcus wrote:
> Actually, the gradient is probably fine, note that he said he was doing linear interpolation.  My guess is Nathan is doing something like:
>
> xm <- x[floor(c)];
> xp <- x[ceil(c)];
> x <- (c - floor(c))*xp + (ceil(c) - c)*xm;
>
> In which case the derivative of x with respect to c is reasonably fine.  The second derivative would be wrong (always = 0) but that's another issue.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
>
>
>
> On Fri, Nov 8, 2013 at 10:17 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > For my particular case, I think the floor calculation should not have a significant effect on the gradient calculation.  The index is just used to look up a value from a table which is applied as a small correction to the model value being compared to the data in the likelihood.  I use the floor loop to find the right index in the table, but then I linearly interpolate between the table values, so I think the gradient should still be smooth.  Also, the correction is just a local variable in the model section, so no sampled parameters are being converted to integers.
> >
> > Your correction may very well be smooth, but calculating it this way lose the gradient information of the correction so even if the posterior is calculated correction its gradient won't.  In the end the Metropolis/slice procedure will correct for any error,
> > but whenever the correction becomes important then the error will induce small acceptance probabilities and poor sampling.  That's the biggest concern.
> >

messages.body_plain:
Ideally, int[] would be promoted to real[] everywhere, but
we aren't quite there yet.  That would create the function

  real mean(int[]);

This is because we promote arguments, but we do not demote return
results.  This is the right behavior here, too, because the
sample mean of a collection of ints is not necessarily an int.

- Bob

I just created an issue for completing the int[] to real[] promotions
in argument position.

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/830

This will not change any return types.  In some cases, we have
specialized functions for int array inputs.  For example, max
has two signatures:

   (int[]):int
   (real[]):real

so we wouldn't promote the int[] to real[] and return real,
but stick with the specialized signature that's already there.

I think I'll hold off on updating the manual.  Adding the promotions
shouldn't be too difficult and there would be a lot of places to
put that hint for now.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
You're right on both counts.  There's no element-wise
exponentiation of row vectors.  And we missed "operator^" in
the index.  I'll add it to the next release of the manual:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/786#issuecomment-51396580

You'll find the more informal doc in the v2.4 manual for ^ on p. 181
under "exponentiation" and in the table of operators.  It doesn't
apply to vectors at all at the moment.

You can just assign to a local variable in a loop, though --- it's no slower in Stan,
just more painful to write.  And in your case, you wouldn't want to
do

>       prob[t] <- dot_product(M[sub,t],a[t]^d[sub]) / ( sum(a[t]^d[sub]) + machine_precision() );

anyway, because that'd require a[t]^d[sub] to be computed twice,
with twice as much work required for the gradients.

For efficiency, it helps to assign complicated subexpressions to
local variables and reuse them.   In this case, the best way to write
this is as:

  {
    vector[K] ad;
    real sum_ad;
    sum_ad <- 0;
    for (int k in 1:K) {
      ad[k] <- a[t,k] ^ d[sub,k];
    sum_ad_pp <- sum(ad) + machine_precision();
    ...
    prob[t] <- dot_product(M[sub,t],ad[k]) / sum_ad_pp;
  }

Even though it's ugly, there's no way around having to define ad in
a local variable like this.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Request for clarification: constraints in data block
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Request for clarification: constraints in data block
messages.body_plain:
On Aug 7, 2014, at 5:25 PM, Jonathan Gilligan <jonathan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> How should I think about constraints on variables declared in the data block?
>
> I am reading chapter 6 of the manual, on time-series modeling, and note that in the MA(2) and MA(Q) models (Sect. 6.3, pp. 46-48), the dimension of the data vector is constrained:
>
> data {
> int<lower=3> T;
> vector[T] y;
> ...
> }
>
> and
> data {
> int<lower=0> Q;
> int<lower=3> T;
> vector[T] y;
>
> In section 3.2 on constrained data types the manual says that constraints are very significant on variables declared in the parameter block, but implies that in the data block they only provide an error check on the data at initialization.

For the parameters, they define transforms plus Jacobians that
define the space over which sampling is actually done.  There the
constraints have to be at least as strict as the support of the model.

For the data block, it's just error checking.

Setting a minimum of T=3 in the MA(2) model makes sure there's at least
one data point.  It technically could be T=2 without causing an error
because Stan's "for (t in 3:T)" does not behave like R's, so that if
T < 3, there are no loop iterations, rather than going backward from
3 down to T like R does.

> I also notice that the manual is somewhat  loose in the constraints in the data block (e.g., often constraining the minimum length of data vectors to be zero, even though a minimum length of 1 would seem more strictly necessary; setting the minimum length of the data vector for an MA(Q) model to 3, when (Q+1) would seem to be necessary, etc.),

That was just sloppiness.  I'll fix it in the next manual and
clarify the above.

>  whereas the manual emphasizes that it is important that constraints in the parameter block be strict in the sense of forbidding any values of parameters outside the domain of the model's support. This distinction reinforces my sense that data constraints don't really affect model performance.

Correct --- it's just error checking that's evaluated once on data input.

> But since I'm not certain about this I would like to ask for clarification: Are there optimizations or other performance-related things that make use of constraints in the data block (and similarly, in the transformed_data, transformed_parameters, and generated_quantities blocks) or are they strictly for error checking the input?

No --- strictly for error checking.

- Bob

messages.subject: Dealing with partially observed ranked observations
messages.subject_clean: Dealing with partially observed ranked observations
messages.body_plain:
This is more of a statistics question than a Stan question per se, although ultimately my model will be done in JAGS or Stan and so this actually goes to the algorithm/code to be written.

Problem setup

Suppose I am interviewing N candidates for job offers.  I have Nstaff staff members who interview these candidates.  Each candidate is not seen by each staff member.  That is, Nobs[1:N] is the number of times a candidate is interviewed by each of the [1:Nstaff] staff members, and Nobs[i] < Nstaff.

In fact, each staff member typically only interviews a relatively small fraction of the candidates (maybe less than half).  You ask the staff members to rank the candidates from 1 (best) to X, where X is the number of people they saw.

The question is: what is the best ordering of candidates, from 1 to N?

Approach + the issue

If each staff member interviewed all candidates then this problem is solved by the Thurstonian model - see http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thurstonian_model.  However the issue I have here is that each staff member does not see all candidates.

For example, suppose there are 20 candidates, and one staff member sees 7 candidates.  You can assume that the quality of the candidates is not correlated with the particular staff member.  The 7 candidates the staff member may be bunched towards the top, so the "1,2,3,4,5,6,7" rankings may be nearer the top end.  But they could also be evenly spread, or they could be near the bottom.

How can I take the ranks of each staff member ([1:Nobs[i]]) and map them to the [1:N] scale.  Does this require some sort of cumulative link ordered response model?

Many thanks

at the point it's used.  You can use print-based debugging to
see what's going wrong.  If you print lp__ (ignore the warnings)
after each statement, you should be able to see where things go wrong.

messages.body_plain:
There's a huge literature on voting that I don't know, and
it depends what you mean by "best" ordering.  Not every way
of sorting is going to give you the same answer.

Partial observations don't prevent you from using the
Thurstonian model.   Each rater has an underlying position
for each object they rate, based on "measurement error" from
the true value, as usual, and that gives you the observed ranking,
as usual.  The only difference is that not every rater ranks
every item.

Stan and JAGS would code these differently.  In Stan, each rater
would get an ordered vector based on their number of observations.
In JAGS, you need to do the Chib/Albert-style truncation trick.

I would, perhaps not surprisingly, recommend building a hierarchical
model for the noise.  And you have to be careful with identifiability
of the underlying true scalars, because there's both an additive
and multiplicative non-identifiability involved.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bob - thanks for the rapid reply.

There is a good article at http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23539504 which has an attachment (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4015936/bin/pone.0096431.s001.pdf) showing JAGS code for a Thurstonian model.

I understand how this model works for the fully observed case.  But how do you treat the case where some people are not observed.

In line with that article, assume that the latent allocation for each item (in this context, a person) is mu[i].  The model assumes that each jth person generates a mental sample as x[i,j] ~ normal(mu[i], sigma[j]).   Here, i is in [1,N] and j is in [1:Nstaff].  This is then compared to actual rankings for each person, y[1:N, 1:Nstaff].  How do you deal with the fact that some staff members are not observed?  For the jth staff member, the y vector has a N rows.  In my example, each person only provides X[j] < N rows.   You can certainly put the [1:X[j]] rankings in y[1:N,j] in the correct positions, and (in JAGS) put NA values in the other positions.  But these rankings will max out at X[j] < N.  Doesn't this screw the algorithm up?

Thanks

On Friday, 8 August 2014 10:01:20 UTC+10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> There's a huge literature on voting that I don't know, and
> it depends what you mean by "best" ordering.  Not every way
> of sorting is going to give you the same answer.
>
> Partial observations don't prevent you from using the
> Thurstonian model.   Each rater has an underlying position
> for each object they rate, based on "measurement error" from
> the true value, as usual, and that gives you the observed ranking,
> as usual.  The only difference is that not every rater ranks
> every item.
>
> Stan and JAGS would code these differently.  In Stan, each rater
> would get an ordered vector based on their number of observations.
> In JAGS, you need to do the Chib/Albert-style truncation trick.
>
> I would, perhaps not surprisingly, recommend building a hierarchical
> model for the noise.  And you have to be careful with identifiability
> of the underlying true scalars, because there's both an additive
> and multiplicative non-identifiability involved.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On Aug 7, 2014, at 7:26 PM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> >
> > This is more of a statistics question than a Stan question per se, although ultimately my model will be done in JAGS or Stan and so this actually goes to the algorithm/code to be written.
> >
> > Problem setup
> >
> > Suppose I am interviewing N candidates for job offers.  I have Nstaff staff members who interview these candidates.  Each candidate is not seen by each staff member.  That is, Nobs[1:N] is the number of times a candidate is interviewed by each of the [1:Nstaff] staff members, and Nobs[i] < Nstaff.
> >
> > In fact, each staff member typically only interviews a relatively small fraction of the candidates (maybe less than half).  You ask the staff members to rank the candidates from 1 (best) to X, where X is the number of people they saw.
> >
> > The question is: what is the best ordering of candidates, from 1 to N?
> >
> > Approach + the issue
> >
> > If each staff member interviewed all candidates then this problem is solved by the Thurstonian model - see http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thurstonian_model.  However the issue I have here is that each staff member does not see all candidates.
> >
> > For example, suppose there are 20 candidates, and one staff member sees 7 candidates.  You can assume that the quality of the candidates is not correlated with the particular staff member.  The 7 candidates the staff member may be bunched towards the top, so the "1,2,3,4,5,6,7" rankings may be nearer the top end.  But they could also be evenly spread, or they could be near the bottom.
> >
> > How can I take the ranks of each staff member ([1:Nobs[i]]) and map them to the [1:N] scale.  Does this require some sort of cumulative link ordered response model?
> >
> > Many thanks
> >

messages.body_plain:
Hi at all,

I have written a Stan-code to sample from a distribution, which has normally around 50 parameters. Because the function to sample from is pretty complex, I have written two codes expressing the function in two different ways. Both codes compile, run and provide output-files. I checked both codes with the built-in diagnostic tool: the error of the gradient lies for each parameter in both codes in the order of e-10 - e-07 (see attachments: *_diagnostics).

With the optimization tool I get for each code a log probability of around 70, but the highest log probability within the samples are mostly still negative (e.g. -18). That is not satisfying.

A much greater problem is the fact, that in the sample output file the 25. parameter is recorded only incompletely and the following parameters are totally lost. In the old fashioned style I printed the "lost" parameters during sampling on the screen and found that they definitely exist on run-time and are not NaN. Has somebody had the same problems with lost parameters? What could be the problem?

My next question concerns the two codes. Because the log likelihood function is pretty complex, the first code calculates the log likelihood in statement separated steps (see attachment: FRETnps_seq.stan). This means that the parameters are used already before the log probability is sampled/calculated. Is this even possible or in/correct?

Because I had doubts in this, I produced a second code in which the increment_log_prob-function explicitly contains/depends on the (transformed) parameters. But this leads to an ugly code (see attachment: FRETnps_one.stan).

Because I have no clue when the sampling step takes place, I'm still not sure which way is the correct one.

The next problem concerns the priors. In our case the number of priors can change in each scenario. That is why I have to read the number of position priors from the data sheet and declare an array of this length. Because each prior in the array has different bounds (but this is not supported by Stans modelling language) each one is bounded from 0 to 1. The individual prior borders are read from the data sheet and the priors are subsequently transformed in a new array. Is this way of dealing with highly divers priors correct or is there another better way?

Because all our priors are flat I just bounded them, what should lead to uniform priors!? Is this correct?

I appreciate any kind of help!

Best regards

Tobias

messages.subject: Re: double mixture model
messages.subject_clean: double mixture model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,

Looking at your code, it seems you are using discrete-valued parameters, which causes Stan's sampler to degenerate into a random walk. I'm also not sure you got the mixture model coded right. You are simply adding up log-probabilities, whereas one would expect something like "for i in 1:N increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(theta[i]) + lp_parts[i,1], log1m(theta[i]) + lp_parts[i,2])))". Here, index i represents an individual, and the second index represents a mixture component (a possible discrete outcome).

Maybe the code you have  is a result of literally translating JAGS/BUGS (which only uses conditional probabilities) to Stan (which requires the full joint posterior to be specified)?

You should drop all discrete parameters and marginalize over all possible (combinations of) discrete values in a loop, save the log-posterior in a temporary variable for each of those combinations, and then use log_sum_exp() and a vector of estimated probabilities (a simplex for each person) to weigh the log-posteriors of each mixture component. The estimates for the values of simplex will then tell you what the probabilities is in what group a person is. You may want to check the Stan manual chapter on mixture models as well. It has some example code.

Best,

Luc

thanks for the suggestion. I change my R code and sample the initial values from a beta(30,30) distribution now. Almost all values are between 0.4-0.6, none is below 0.2 or above 0.8. I ran it 3 times, but I am still getting the same error message on every run.

Is there a particular reason, why you don't use beta distributions with Stan? Are they somehow implemented differently than in BUGS/JAGS? Most of my parameters have a natural boundaries of 0 and 1 and I like the flexibility of the beta distribution in that it can accommodate very skewed data. Or would you suggest to use a different distribution?

Thanks a lot,
Jan

> Christian Roy
> August 8, 2014 at 5:29 PM

> Hi Jan,
>
> By experience the error message "Rejecting user-specified initialization because of vanishing density" is due to bad initialization values. I triggered this error message in the past by creating starting values that created -inf values on the log scale or on the logit scale.
>
> Your model seems to use the beta distribution. I never used the beta distribution with Stan but based on my experience with JAGS and WinBUGS I would guess that your initialization values a probably too close to zero for some parameters. You may want to try starting values that are away from zero to see if you can get the model over the bump.
>
> HTH
>
> Chris

I know that is maybe asking too much, because you developers have already done so much, but maybe this could be a community effort (I would certainly be willing to contribute.)

messages.body_plain:
Thanks.

That's definitely a parsing bug.  The exponentiation operator currently
has the wrong precedence --- it should bind less tightly than indexing.
I created a high-priority issue to fix it with a simplified model:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/834

For now, you'll have to use pow() or wrap the arguments to the ^ operator
in parens; e.g., (a[1])^(b[1]).

- Bob

First, I will create an appendix for the manual listing the error
messages and trying to explain them better.  The problem is that they
can often come from multiple sources.  The "vanishing density" and
"informational message" messages are the ones users are most often
confused about.  We'd ideally like to make the messages themselves better
rather than requiring a trip back to the manual, but that's harder than
it sounds --- we've never had any luck explaining the informational message
and users continue to construe it as a bug rather than a warning, no matter
how we word it.  We're taking another pass in the next release.

We do have beta distributions and Stan and would use them wherever
appropriate.  The reason you don't see us coding models the same way
as in JAGS is due to a number of reasons.  First, there's no benefit to conjugate
priors in Stan models, so we don't use a lot of inverse gamma or Wisharts,
as there are better approaches.  Second, for uniform distributions on bounded
variables, we don't need a prior --- it's already uniform.  So you don't
see beta(1,1) used anywhere as it's redundant.  Third, we often work with
GLMs rather than straight up binomial parameters, and those don't involve
beta densities.  But by all means use them if they make sense for your model.
We also don't use a lot of Dirichlet priors, but that's because they're very
weak in not specifying any covariance structure.

Have you tried my suggestion of trying to diagnose where the log prob
goes to -infinity by using print("lp__=",lp__) statements?

Your code's too long for me to try to debug by inspection, but you should
also make sure to define every variable before you use it --- the order
of statements matters in Stan.  And make sure every argument is legal to
every function called.

I'd also be careful about your T[L,U].  That's not necessary in Stan
if L and U are constants and the variable is already constrained to lie
between L and U.  You have a problem in that you define

real<lower=0,upper=1> foo;

and then pair that with

 foo ~ beta(alpha,beta) T[0.001,0.999];

This is a very bad thing to do in Stan because the constraint on
the variable foo ([0,1]) does not match the support of the
distribution specified, which is truncated to [0.001,0.999].

- Bob

On Aug 8, 2014, at 11:14 AM, Tobias Eilert <tobias.e...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi at all,
>
> I have written a Stan-code to sample from a distribution, which has normally around 50 parameters. Because the function to sample from is pretty complex, I have written two codes expressing the function in two different ways. Both codes compile, run and provide output-files. I checked both codes with the built-in diagnostic tool: the error of the gradient lies for each parameter in both codes in the order of e-10 - e-07 (see attachments: *_diagnostics).
>
> With the optimization tool I get for each code a log probability of around 70, but the highest log probability within the samples are mostly still negative (e.g. -18). That is not satisfying.

Maybe not, but are you sure it's wrong?  Often the optimized log density
is much higher than the density in the typical set.  In very pathological
cases, such as sampling from beta(0.5,0.5), you'll find the optimizer
gets nearly infinite density before it halts, whereas the sampler will
be much better behaved.

> A much greater problem is the fact, that in the sample output file the 25. parameter is recorded only incompletely and the following parameters are totally lost. In the old fashioned style I printed the "lost" parameters during sampling on the screen and found that they definitely exist on run-time and are not NaN. Has somebody had the same problems with lost parameters? What could be the problem?

Nobody's reported losing parameters except in cases where the
program does not terminate normally.  Did the program exit normally or
was there something that crashed it?   Does the same thing happen
every time?  If it happens every time (crash or no), could you let me know
which model and which data to run to reproduce the problem?

> My next question concerns the two codes. Because the log likelihood function is pretty complex, the first code calculates the log likelihood in statement separated steps (see attachment: FRETnps_seq.stan). This means that the parameters are used already before the log probability is sampled/calculated. Is this even possible or in/correct?

Every variable must be defined (not just declared) before it is used.
Parameters are automatically defined, as are data variables if you get
past init.  All other variables (transformed data, transformed parameters,
local variables) must be defined before they are used.

> Because I had doubts in this, I produced a second code in which the increment_log_prob-function explicitly contains/depends on the (transformed) parameters. But this leads to an ugly code (see attachment: FRETnps_one.stan).
>
> Because I have no clue when the sampling step takes place, I'm still not sure which way is the correct one.

There's a pretty complete description in the manual in the part
on the language describing what happens in each block.  See
chapter 18, "Execution of a Stan Program" for an overview, then
the rest of that part for complete (I hope!) details.

> The next problem concerns the priors. In our case the number of priors can change in each scenario. That is why I have to read the number of position priors from the data sheet and declare an array of this length. Because each prior in the array has different bounds (but this is not supported by Stans modelling language) each one is bounded from 0 to 1. The individual prior borders are read from the data sheet and the priors are subsequently transformed in a new array. Is this way of dealing with highly divers priors correct or is there another better way?

If you transform a variable then used the transformed variable on the
left side of the sampling ~, you need to include the log Jacobian determinants.
There are details in the manual chapter 13, "Reparameterizations & Change of Variables".

> Because all our priors are flat I just bounded them, what should lead to uniform priors!? Is this correct?

The default priors are uniform on the support of variables.  If the
variables are bounded above and below, the priors will be proper.
Stan does not require proper priors, but does require proper posteriors.

- Bob

Hi Jan,

The only reason I  have never used the beta distribution in Stan is because I used the beta distribution to estimate detection in occupancy modelling or abundance modelling and it's impossible to do those kind of model in Stan (for the moment...maybe forever....but I keep dreaming that it will be possible one day).

I've never worked with the type of model you are using right now but I think the problem is that your starting values are actually defining the parameters of some of your beta distribution.

For example "r_a" is a parameter for a beta distribution in the model.

yet "r_a" is the product itself of "r_mu" and "r_kappa"  and r_kappa" itself is defined from "r_prime_kappa".

So even if you try to keep your values away from the extreme you could end up with some kind of highly constrained beta distribution (multiplying a lot of values between 0 and 1 is bound to create some problem at some point).

Basically I feel like the model will be really tricky to initialize no matter what software you use.

I have some really painful memories of trying to initialize models like that in JAGS. In those situation I usually started backward. I created a function that would define the most troublesome values and derive the hyper priors from those values.

 Chris
