messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dealing with partially observed ranked observations
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Dealing with partially observed ranked observations
messages.body_plain:
On Aug 7, 2014, at 9:26 PM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Bob - thanks for the rapid reply.
>
> There is a good article at http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23539504 which has an attachment (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4015936/bin/pone.0096431.s001.pdf) showing JAGS code for a Thurstonian model.
>
> I understand how this model works for the fully observed case.  But how do you treat the case where some people are not observed.
>
> In line with that article, assume that the latent allocation for each item (in this context, a person) is mu[i].  The model assumes that each jth person generates a mental sample as x[i,j] ~ normal(mu[i], sigma[j]).

That makes sense other than that I wouldn't use the variable "x" for
a parameter --- it violate's Andrew's conventions that "x" is for unmodeled
data, "y" for data, and greek letters for parameters.

Then you need to fix the location and scale of mu for identifiability --- the
model you sent uses normal(0,0.001) in JAGS, which is equivalent to normal(0,sqrt(1000))
in Stan.  I'd just use normal(0,1) to make sure the scale of sigma lined up properly.
the numbers easier to scan --- the scale doesn't matter (except in its interaction
with the scale of sigma).

I'd also be inclined to build a hierarchical model for the sigma[j], but that's
another issue.

> Here, i is in [1,N]  and j is in [1:Nstaff].  This is then compared to actual rankings for each person, y[1:N, 1:Nstaff].  How do you deal with the fact that some staff members are not observed?  For the jth staff member, the y vector has a N rows.  In my example, each person only provides X[j] < N rows.   You can certainly put the [1:X[j]] rankings in y[1:N,j] in the correct positions, and (in JAGS) put NA values in the other positions.  But these rankings will max out at X[j] < N.  Doesn't this screw the algorithm up?

The model you sent me is wrong in the text that the rank needs to be something
like

  y[j,] <- rank(x[j,])

You can't call rank(x[j,i]) because x[j,i] is a scalar!

I also don't think their JAGS code is going to be efficient because
they're using the dinterval trick for rejection, when they could just
use truncation a la Albert-Chib.

All you need to do for your model where not every individual i
is observed is to trim the implicit rankings down to the ones you observe:

  y[j,] <- trim(y[j,],rank(x[j,]));

where the "trim" function just chops the result down to the individuals
for which you have observations, which are just the ones in y[j,].
(I know "trim" isn't a built-in function in anyone's system.)

The hard part is going to be coding it in either Stan or JAGS.
If all the y[i,] are the same size, it's easy.  If everything was observed
in Stan, this model's trivial to code:

data {
  int<lower=0> I;  // number of items being ranked
  int<lower=0> J;  // number of raters
  int<lower=1,upper=I> y[J,I];   // ranks for rater j
}
parameters {
  real mu[I];                        // true latent positions
  real<lower=0,upper=20> sigma[J];   // accuracy of rater j
  ordered[I] x[J];                   // positions assigned by rater j
}
model {
  mu ~ normal(0,1000);
  for (j in 1:J)
    for (i in 1:I)
      x[j,i] ~ normal(mu[i],sigma[j]);
}

The ordered[I] data type is for I ordered values.  This is
the appropriate constraint on the underlying values (though it
makes lower better --- you'd have to reverse to get it the other
way around because ordered sorts in ascending order).

I think this is much simpler than you see in the JAGS encoding in the
referenced PDF (though as I said, I don't think this is the best JAGS
encoding --- the alternative would involve truncated normal sampling
statements in JAGS).

If each rater rates the same number of items, say K, then all you
need to do to code in Stan is to add a variable for K, replace y[J,I] with
y[J,K] and ordered[I]  with ordered[K] in the declarations and then loop
from 1:K rather than 1:I in the model.  The truncations you'd need in
JAGS (or rejections the way the example was coded in the PDF) automatically
get handled by the ordered vector data type.

If not every rater rates the same number of items, then the model's
going to be difficult to code because neither Stan nor JAGS supports
ragged arrays.  And Stan doesn't support ragged constraints.  So you'd
need to either (a) break the data down ahead of time into groups with
the same number of observations, then proceed as above [although it's
hard to make general], or (b) bite the bullet and code up ragged data
structures (using the trick described in the manual for LDA or naive
Bayes) and define the transforms and Jacobians yourself (they're simple
for the ordered vectors --- see the last chapter of the manual on
variable transforms).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Silly me --- Martin is the one who is coding these models for Erik-Jan!
So I guess that one's not done yet.  My question does still stand
about releasing the models.  It'd be very helpful to Stan users.

The Google books link doesn't work --- it just appears to give
me pages unavailable in a Slavic language (doesn't look
like Dutch despite being on the .nl domain).  But the pdf of the
first two parts, including the relevant pages, are available straight
from the authors:

  https://webfiles.uci.edu/mdlee/LeeWagenmakers2013_Free.pdf

Do you know what the MCMC std error is for JAGS?  And are you sure
it converged?  The MCMC std err is reported under se_mean for Stan.
It'd be good to rule out sampling error as the source of any differences.

I'd also suggest simulating some data according to the model and fitting
that.  Then you'd know if you're getting the right answers (to within
sampling uncertainty, of course).

As of yet, we haven't found models where we can't fit the same
answers as JAGS, which increases my confidence in both systems (though
Michael will probably scold me for saying so).

You definitely want to follow Herra Huu's advice and use log_sum_exp()
and log1m() for numerical stability and for efficiency.

And unless you need lp_parts in the output, I'd just define a single
lp_parts 4-vector as a local in the model and reuse it, replacing

transformed parameters {
  vector[4] lp_parts[nx, nz];
  for (i in 1:nx) {
    for (j in 1:nz) {
      lp_parts[i, j, 1] <- (log1m(x_prob[i]) + log1m(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], alpha));
      lp_parts[i, j, 2] <- (log(x_prob[i]) + log(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], alpha));
      lp_parts[i, j, 3] <- (log1m(x_prob[i]) + log(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], beta));
      lp_parts[i, j, 4] <- (log(x_prob[i]) + log1m(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], beta));
    }
  }
}
model {
  for (i in 1:nx)
    for (j in 1:nz)
      increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp_parts[i,j]));
}

with

model {
  vector[4] lp_parts;

  for (i in 1:nx) {
    for (j in 1:nz) {

      lp_parts[1] <- (log1m(x_prob[i]) + log1m(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], alpha));
      lp_parts[2] <- (log(x_prob[i]) + log(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], alpha));
      lp_parts[3] <- (log1m(x_prob[i]) + log(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], beta));
      lp_parts[4] <- (log(x_prob[i]) + log1m(z_prob[j]) + bernoulli_log(k[i, j], beta));
      increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp_parts));
    }
  }
}

It'd be even more efficient without the bernoulli_log, taking
log(alpha), log1m(alpha), log(beta), and log1m(beta) outside the
loop and reusing inside the loop based on switching on the value of k[i,j].
It'd make the model even harder to read, though, so I wouldn't recommend it
unless you really need to scale this and it's not fast enough as is.

Why not just use x_prob and y_prob for inference?  These are the probabilities
for the individuals and questions being in each class, and it's more efficient
to use probabilities for inference (posterior expectations) than samples (posterior
samples).

Otherwise, the model as coded in Stan above looks right to me (given Martin's
data and parameter declarations).

- Bob

I didn't have a lot of trouble initializing this model in JAGS, but I wonder if the initialization would benefit, if I'd sample the parameter of the group distribution in the model block not from an uninformative beta(1,1), but rather a more symmetrical beta(10,10, or beta(20,20) even though this might entail running the sample for a bit longer until convergence is reached. Hang on!  It's not impossible to do these kinds of models in Stan.
We've fit all kinds of discrete population models.  For example,
there are some defined in this branch:

feature/issue-451-mark-recapture-egs

You can view it using GitHub's online viewer:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/feature/issue-451-mark-recapture-egs/src/models/misc

The examples are in src/models/misc under mark-recapture and occupancy directories.

We also have models that Fraenzi Korner-Nievergelt generalized for us as
part of her book on population models.

What is impossible is doing it with discrete parameters.  But
if you can marginalize out the discrete parameters, it's much more
efficient to sample these models in Stan.

I need to add some more examples to the manual!

extreme initial values.

If the initialization works in JAGS, it should work in Stan.
My guess is that there's a bug in your Stan code for the model
that's causing the log prob to be -infinity.  A likely cause is
not having all variables defined.

I would very very strongly suggest following my earlier advice
and trying to track down where the model goes bad using print()
statements.

- Bob

> > For example "r_a" is a parameter for a beta distribution in the model.

Hi Fei,

Within CmdStan, it's really, really easy to update Stan. Here are two options:
1) From CmdStan, when calling make, set the STAN_HOME variable to your existing Stan folder. So, something like: "make STAN_HOME=/usr/daniel/dev/stan/ foo" where foo.stan is the model. Note: it needs the trailing forward slash.
2) From CmdStan, instead of setting the STAN_HOME variable, which defaults to "stan/", just make edits to the copy of Stan inside CmdStan.

Both options above also work when you're using git to manage branches.

Daniel

> confused about.  We'd ideally like to make the messages themselves better
> rather than requiring a trip back to the manual, but that's harder than
> it sounds --- we've never had any luck explaining the informational message
> and users continue to construe it as a bug rather than a warning, no matter
> how we word it.  We're taking another pass in the next release.
>
> We do have beta distributions and Stan and would use them wherever
> appropriate.  The reason you don't see us coding models the same way
> as in JAGS is due to a number of reasons.  First, there's no benefit to conjugate
> priors in Stan models, so we don't use a lot of inverse gamma or Wisharts,
> as there are better approaches.  Second, for uniform distributions on bounded
> variables, we don't need a prior --- it's already uniform.  So you don't
> see beta(1,1) used anywhere as it's redundant.  Third, we often work with
> GLMs rather than straight up binomial parameters, and those don't involve
> beta densities.  But by all means use them if they make sense for your model.
> We also don't use a lot of Dirichlet priors, but that's because they're very
> weak in not specifying any covariance structure.
>
> Have you tried my suggestion of trying to diagnose where the log prob
> goes to -infinity by using print("lp__=",lp__) statements?
>
> Your code's too long for me to try to debug by inspection, but you should
> also make sure to define every variable before you use it --- the order
> of statements matters in Stan.  And make sure every argument is legal to
> every function called.
>
> I'd also be careful about your T[L,U].  That's not necessary in Stan
> if L and U are constants and the variable is already constrained to lie
> between L and U.  You have a problem in that you define
>
> real<lower=0,upper=1> foo;
>
> and then pair that with
>
>  foo ~ beta(alpha,beta) T[0.001,0.999];
>
> This is a very bad thing to do in Stan because the constraint on
> the variable foo ([0,1]) does not match the support of the
> distribution specified, which is truncated to [0.001,0.999].

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I've seen a bit of discussion about the scalability of Stan (including a nice plot by Bob C., I think) with big data.  And, I've found a few threads about Stan and MPI / OpenMP (pun intended).  Still, I'm not clear on whether Stan can farm out computations across processors/cores, as might be done with a large number of conditionally independent, e.g., likelihood factors. To be clear, I'm not talking about the relatively popular Stan topic of parallel chains, but more along the lines of parallelizing computations within iterations.  I anticipate data sets on the order of 10^5 or 10^6 observations (tree rings, btw), and I wonder how Stan will handle such big data.  More specifically, can Stan leverage a large number of cores (not for parallel chains necessarily!)?

Best,

Jarrett

messages.body_plain:
10^6 isn't that much data, but it depends what you do with it.

We don't have any immediate plans to parallelize computations
within chains, though we are well aware of the potential benefits
and trends in computing.  The real puzzle is how we could deal with
autodiff, which requires substantial synchronization.

One thing we might be able to do is parallelize matrix operations.
For most of them, we're just operating on double values and
computing analytic derivatives, which we piece back together.
That'd only help with big matrices.

The other alternative would be to break down functions into
blocks that have independent gradients, then we can compute the
block and get its partials, then put everything back together.
We haven't even begun to think about how to do that --- I don't
see how we could write a smart enough compiler to do it
automatically.

- Bob

Thank you for all replies.

Bob:
Yes Bob, it's me who is coding for E.J. :)  I haven't been working on it for a while and now I'm trying to finish the task. I believe that the models will be released publicly then, since BUGS and JAGS codes are public.

1} Do you know what the MCMC std error is for JAGS?  And are you sure it converged?  The MCMC std err is reported under se_mean for Stan.

It'd be good to rule out sampling error as the source of any differences.

Jags is not reporting std. error, but is reporting this:

DIC info (using the rule, pD = var(deviance)/2)
pD = 2.3 and DIC = 33.3
DIC is an estimate of expected predictive error (lower deviance is better).

I tried to run Jags with higher iterations, different initials and inspecting traceplot... And it always converges to the values I posted before.

2} I'd also suggest simulating some data according to the model and fitting that.  Then you'd know if you're getting the right answers (to within sampling uncertainty, of course).

Ok, I just tried both models on simulated data and the Stan model is way off while Jags model shines.

3) You definitely want to follow Herra Huu's advice and use log_sum_exp() and log1m() for numerical stability and for efficiency. And unless you need lp_parts in the output, I'd just define a single lp_parts 4-vector as a local in the model and reuse it, replacing

My logic for not using log_sum_exp() here is that I would exp variable lp_parts at the beginning so I won't have to do it again in generated quantities. There I'm using lp_parts to identify mixing probabilities. Or is there a better way to do this? So it means that I would exponentiate it twice - once in log_sum_exp and once in generated quantities. And I would also have to add a few lines and maybe a variable too.
And that's also reason why I'm not having lp_parts as local variable.

4) Why not just use x_prob and y_prob for inference?  These are the probabilities for the individuals and questions being in each class, and it's more efficient

to use probabilities for inference (posterior expectations) than samples (posterior samples).

That's an overall quantity, but what I'm looking for is the per-parameter
MCMC std error, which is

   se = sd / sqrt(n_eff)

where sd is posterior standard deviation and n_eff is the number of effective
samples.

I'm surprised Coda doesn't provide it, as it's the main thing you want to use
to determine if you have enough posterior effective samples.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: double mixture model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: double mixture model
messages.body_plain:
I realized what the problem is.  The "double mixture" part!

The overall model probability is

 p(alpha,beta,x,z,theta,k)
   = Uniform(alpha|0,1)
     * Uniform(beta|0,alpha)
     * PROD_{i in 1:I} Bernoulli(x[i] | 0.5)
     * PROD_{j in 1:J} Bernoulli(z[j] | 0.5)
     * PROD_{i in 1:I} PROD_{j in 1:J} Bernoulli(k[i,j] | x[i] == z[j] ? alpha : beta)

The problem is that you can't independently model the each (i,j) pair -- they
are all dependent through the x[i] and z[j].  That is, each x[i] applies
to all j in 1:J, and each z[j] needs to apply to all x[i] for i in 1:8.

There are 2^8 possible values for x and 2^8 possible values for z in
this tiny tiny example, but already that's 2^16, or about 64000, summands.

I don't think there's any way to code this model efficiently in Stan.
You can just sum over the 2^16 values of x, z, but that's going to be
very painful to code, slow to run, and not scalable.  On the other hand,
it'll probably be more efficient at estimating the tails than the model
in JAGS.

- Bob

You can do this in Stan in the first dimensions, but not
arbitrary dimensions.  So if the last two dimensions of x
were swapped, you can write head(x[5,5],20) for what
would be x[5,5,1:20] in R.

Generalizing these capabilities is on the to-do list.

Writing loops to do this in Stan is fast, though clunky.  There's
no advantage to vectorizing assignnents in Stan --- just sampling
statements or other arithmetic going into log prob calculations
because it's involved in gradients, which can often be partially
evaluated (i.e., unfolded with the chain rule) in vectorized
operations.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for sending the detailed reports and working code.

As far as I can tell, the Stan program is a faithful translation
of the log probability function defined by the model.

I'm running the example now and it's super slow, both in
terms of iteration time and number of effective samples per
iteration.  And if you do this:

head(get_sampler_params(samples,inc_warmup=FALSE)[[1]],n=100)

you'll see that n_divergent=1 for every iteration, which is
signalling a problem with the log probability during sampling (you
want n_divergent=0 for every iteration).

The problem is in the posterior.

Non-differentiable "link" functions are bad news, particularly
in Stan, which relies on derivatives.  The link here for the
binomial parameter theta[i,j] is

   theta[i, j] <- fmin(1.0, exp(-alpha[i] * t[j]) + beta[i]);

If alpha[i], beta[i] and t[j] are such that you get the 1.0
branch of fmin(), you lose all connection to the parameters in the model in
the neighborhood of the parameter values.  For Stan this is bad because
without gradients, it devolves to a random walk.

What were the JAGS fits for the model in terms of alpha and beta?

I'd have tried to formulate this model using a differentiable link
function rather than f(u) = fmin(1,u).  inv_logit is a typical choice,
which would set

   theta[i, j] <- inv_logit(exp(-alpha[i] * t[j]) + beta[i]);

It's not a pure exponential decay, though.

Then you could also leave alpha and beta unconstrained --- I don't
understand why they're fixed in the current approach anyway, other than
to keep them near a range where the expression doesn't exceed 1.

Another thing you could do would be to put a constraint on beta
that kept it below max(exp(-alpha[i] * t)).  The problem is that we can't declare
varying constraints, so it'd have to be done in a loop including the transform
and Jacobian.  We're going to add in the constraint functions in the future
with built-in Jacobians, at which point this'll get easier.

It might also be convenient to declare theta as matrix[ns - 1, nt - 1] and
alpha and beta as vector[ns - 1].

You don't need to write alpha ~ beta(1,1) --- it's uniform and the default
with no sampling statement provided.   It doesn't hurt to add it --- it just
incurs a couple of runtime checks that values are valid each time the log
prob is evaluated and adds a bit of extra overhead to autodiff.

I wrote a simple model and simulator, and Stan has a hard time fitting
with simulated data and the times given --- it's not much data, and I
don't know what the true posterior is --- the posterior intervals are very
wide, so it's getting the parameters in the posterior intervals at least.

Data simulated from the model doesn't look much like the real data.
This is highly subjective, but the real data asymptotes down to 4 at
different rates for all subjects.  I think it'd be odd to get all those
4s from a binomial model with decay given the width of the intervals
and the exponential model.

- Bob

The function is weird because what I really want is to know if f(x,r) > f(y,r) for some parameter r and data x: bernoulli_logit( scale * (f(x,r) - f(y,r))), where f(x,r) = x^(1-r) / (1-r) . But the function blows up near r=1 because it divides by zero. The special case for "r=1" is to avoid this singularity, and is the standard treatment in the econ literature. I probably should deal with the measure-zero issue by adjusting to use a neighborhood:
>
> if (fabs(r=1.0) < epsilon)
>   return log(x);
> else
>   return pow(x, 1.0 - r) / (1.0 - r);
>
>
> r > 1 (x to a negative power) is not an issue because x >= 0  and I can avoid the x=0 case by adding a small number to make x strictly greater than 0.
>
> If I could avoid r = 1, that would be nice, but the literature reports values that range from 0 to 40 or higher for different conditions and based on a lot of that literature, r=1 is a pretty reasonable mode for a prior.  A published MLE of the data set I'm working with gives a 95% CI of 0.67 to 1.02 for r.

On Aug 11, 2014, at 2:06 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Sunday, August 10, 2014 4:15:03 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> P.S.  I've tried to restrict the term "vectorized" to when
> a function can take a vector for an argument as well as
> a scalar, and that's not what's going on here.  But it's
> used all over in different ways in other packages and by
> other people, so it's probably a hopeless battle to restrict
> its technical meaning.
>
> Can we start calling such functions "vector friendly"? And some vector friendly functions are also "derivative accumulating"?

OK.  And there are really two different ways to be "vector friendly".

1.  the way log(vector) works, is componentwise.  That is, it just
    repeats log on each element.

2.  the way normal_log(vector,...) works, which is to add the result
    for each element together.

Eigen calls the former elementwise operations and the latter reductions.
Some reductions are built-in and not just accumulations over elementwise
definitions, such as sum() and maxCoeff().

> And a small number of for loops in Stan are "batched" by the compiler / processor?

I don't know what this means.

- Bob

On Aug 10, 2014, at 5:40 PM, Jonathan Gilligan <jonathan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks.
>
> I was going to ask a followup about the "r=1" case, but wanted to test the code myself first.
>
> This is a pretty standard utility function from economics, describing constant relative risk-aversion and plausible values span 1. The function is weird because what I really want is to know if f(x,r) > f(y,r) for some parameter r and data x: bernoulli_logit( scale * (f(x,r) - f(y,r))), where f(x,r) = x^(1-r) / (1-r) . But the function blows up near r=1 because it divides by zero. The special case for "r=1" is to avoid this singularity, and is the standard treatment in the econ literature. I probably should deal with the measure-zero issue by adjusting to use a neighborhood:
>
> if (fabs(r=1.0) < epsilon)
>   return log(x);
> else
>   return pow(x, 1.0 - r) / (1.0 - r);
>

this has to be coded with "r == 1.0", but the compiler
will tell you that.

> r > 1 (x to a negative power) is not an issue because x >= 0  and I can avoid the x=0 case by adding a small number to make x strictly greater than 0.

If you have a constraint lower=0 on x, then x will only be 0 if you initialize to
0 (which is an error in most cases) or if there's an underflow.

> If I could avoid r = 1, that would be nice, but the literature reports values that range from 0 to 40 or higher for different conditions and based on a lot of that literature, r=1 is a pretty reasonable mode for a prior.  A published MLE of the data set I'm working with gives a 95% CI of 0.67 to 1.02 for r.
>
> How badly will this function screw up Stan's ability to calculate Jacobians? Do you have any suggestions for how to code something like this efficiently in Stan?

Maybe Michael will know.

I'm not sure where you mean.  The only Jacobian (determinants) we compute
are for the transforms, and that doesn't depend on anything past the
parameters block.

It will screw up gradients at r = 1 as the function's discontinuous.
I'm not sure what happens under the crossing, because of the sign change.
With a fixed x and r = 1 + epsilon, you get a really big value, whereas
with a fixed x and r = 1 - epsilon, you get a really small value.  So the
function's discontinuous at r, which is a problem.  It's impossible to
simulate a particle moving according to the Hamiltonian when it has to
cross a discontinuous boundary.  In fact, we want the derivatives to
be continuous, as well as the function (which is why fabs() can be problematic).

- Bob

> On Sunday, August 10, 2014 3:20:45 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> On Aug 9, 2014, at 1:24 PM, Jonathan Gilligan <jonathan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Two questions about user-defined functions:
> >
> > 1. If the function takes a vector argument, is there a way to get the length of the vector so I can loop over its elements? I would like to do something like this:
> >
> > vector foo(vector x, real r) {
> >    vector bar;
> >
> >    for (i in 1:length(x)) {
> >        bar[i] <- x[i]^(1.-r) / (1.-r);
> >   }
> >   return(bar);
> > }
> >
> > So as a work-around, I'm trying this to exponentiate a vector:
> > vector foo(vector x, real r) {
> >   return exp(log(x) * (1. - r)) / (1. - r);
> > }
> >
> > 2. I am having problems compiling .stan files with user-defined functions. The attached file compiles from .stan to .cpp with no complaints, but the c++ compiler gives me a long and confusing bunch of error messages, of which this seems most germane:
>
> I isolated the bug and created a small reproducible example,
> which I included in the issue along with an explanation:
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/849
>
> For now, you can workaround the bug with this modified function:
>
>   vector eu_item(vector x, real r) {
>     if (r == 1.) {
>       vector[cols(x)] log_x;
>       log_x <- log(x);
>       return log_x;
>       // WAS JUST: return log(x);
>     } else {
>       return exp(log(x) * (1.-r)) / (1.-r); # x^(1.-r) / (1.-r)
>     }
>
> The problem arises in the "return log(x)" when x is data and
> r is a parameter.  The return scalar type for log(x) is double (data),
> but it needs to be promoted to an autodiff variable (parameter).
>
> This should be fixed by the next release.
>
> Having said all this, I think there's going to be an issue with
> your function, because if r is real, it should never be exactly 1,
> as that's a measure 0 subset of the probability mass for it.  So you
> could probably just drop this altogether.
>
> Are there constraints on what r's value should be?  If r > 1, that
> looks like it could be problematic.
>
> - Bob
>

On Aug 10, 2014, at 2:00 AM, Tammo Nikolas <tammo...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I am trying to set up a mixture model in PyStan and I am not sure whether my approach is correct.
>
> I have time series data and I want to fit several models, that may be nested.
> I know that generally none of the models is able to capture all characteristics of the data.
>
> I'd be interested in the posterior likelihood of the model parameters and the model choice,
> in order to see how parameter across-model-means, weighted by the respective model likelihood, perform.
> Therefore I was planning to do something along the lines of what John Kruschke describes as transdimensional MCMC.
> Since this is not possible in Stan, what I want to do is mixture modelling as described in chapter 9 of the tutorial.
>
> So, this is a simple version of it:
>
> data {
>
>     int<lower=1> K; // number of mixing components
>
>     int<lower=0> N; // number of data points
>
>     vector<lower=0>[N] aif;
>
>     positive_ordered[N] time;
>
>     vector[N] data;
>
> }
>
>
>
> parameters {
>
>    simplex[K] w; //Mixing proportions
>    // real<lower=0, upper=1> weight1; //alternative to simplex
>
>
>     real<lower=0.01, upper=3> par1[K]; // model parameter
>
>     real<lower=0.01, upper=.8> par2[K]; // model parameter
>     real<lower=0> sigma[K]
>
> }
>
>
>
> model {
>
>    real ps[K];
>
>    ps[1] <- log(w[1]) + normal_log(data,
>
>                     Model1(time, aif, par1, par2), sigma[1]);
>
>    ps[2] <- log(w[2]) + normal_log(data,
>
>                     Model2(time, aif, par1, par2), sigma[2]);
>
>
>         increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
>
>    }
>
>
> Model1 and Model2 are computationally fairly expensive, separately defined functions.
>
> Does this approach make sense at all for this kind of model?

This is the right way to define a mixture model if you want to generalize
beyond 2 components.

Whether the combination makes sense depends on the data and
what Model1 and Model2 are!

> Is it ok to use normal_log on the vectors (model and data)?

Yes.  See the manual for how this works.  If you have a data
vector y, mean vector mu, and sd scalar sigma, then

   normal_log(y,mu,sd) = SUM_{n in 1:size(y)} normal_log(y[n], mu[n], sd);

So mu and y need to be the same size.  And both must be vectors (not
matrices).

> The results I get for an easy test seem to be correct (see attachment, model paraemters were .7 and .2)
> The only thing that confuses me is, that the wrong (in this example very wrong) model still
> get's a fairly large mixture proportion (mean at about 30% of the right model), as shown in the attached graphical output.
> I would have expected it to be close to zeros, and the w distribution to become more like a delta peak.
> How should I interpret this mixing proportions? They don't seem to allow for something like a weighted mean estimate.
>

How much data did you have and what were the priors?  It takes a lot
of data even to estimate a bernoulli as a sharp peak.

You should explore what the parameters are for model1 and model2 and
perhaps also save the log probabilities in each model and keep them
with the data points and you might see what's going on.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Maybe I missed something in the earlier discussion, but the
CRRA/isoelastic utility function family defined as

log(c)                if r=1
(c^(1-r) - 1)/(1-r)   otherwise

_is_ continuous both in c and r. The standard way of showing this is
using L'Hopital's rule. The -1 in the numerator is important, and seems
to be missing in the definition below.

The function is also continuously differentiable in c (u'(c)=c^(-r)),
and also in r --- this can be shown by calculating

\lim_{r\to1} \frac{(c^(1-r) - 1)/(1-r)-log(c)}{r-1} = -\log^2(c)/2

Best,

Tamas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Clarification on Change of Variables
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Clarification on Change of Variables
messages.body_plain:
Stan only applies Jacobians for implicit transformations
due to constraints on parameters.  Everything else is up to
the user.

It's when the parameters are on the left of the sampling
statements, at least under the usual interpretation of sampling
notation, that you need to add the log Jacobian determinant.

The normal example you provide is subtle because the density
normal(y|mu,sigma) is equivalent to normal(mu|y,sigma).  So
the contribution to the log probability is the same in Stan for

   mu1 * mu2 ~ normal(y, sigma);

and

   y ~ normal(mu1 * mu2, sigma);

But the modeling implication is usually different, with the
former notation implying a Jacobian is required under the
usual interpretation and the latter not requiring it.

- Bob

coefficient (r below) is usually fixed, and affine transformations don't
affect comparisons of utility, so it is common to drop the -1. But it is
needed for a continuous family. On top of that, economists rarely
consider differentiability in the coefficient, I had to do the proof for
continuity myself before posting, just to be sure.

I wonder if this solves the OP's problem.

Best,

Tamas

>

>
> > Thanks for the suggestions.  Using only one scale parameter helped.  In this model (attached), the priors on bi_raw and bi_scale are constrained so that bi + bj will be appropriately ordered.  The item cutpoints are declared and fixed as per your suggestion.  With those changes, STAN is producing fewer errors (just one or two per warm up period per chain).
> >
> > The traces look better than before, but still aren't mixing well (a few from bi are attached).  Rhats are still high, from 1.3 to 20.  However, the bi estimates themselves are generally in the right range.  At least, they tend to be of the same sign as the simulated values.
>
> If the model's converging properly, all R-hat values should be under 1.05,
> and ideally very close to 1.
>
> Very high R-hats often signal non-identifiabilities in the model, especially
> if other parameters do converge reasonably.
>
> > Another possible hiccup is in the response data.  Some simulated respondents never use certain response categories, due to response style.  It would be very difficult to estimate the third threshold (bi[,3]) for someone who never uses the highest response category.  Simulating more extreme vignettes helps, but in the real world there are often respondents with this sort of response data.  It may call for a ragged array.
>
> You just want to be sure to avoid things like separability.  You need
> stronger priors to overcome them and still sample efficiently.
>
> - Bob
>
> >

> > Hmm, it looks like you’re scaling each cutpoint separately, which would seem like it would leave the vector bi[] not being ordered in at least some cases. Shouldn’t you be multiplying by a single value (or a single value per item, at least)?
> >
> > Also, I think that’s not the best way to fix a value for bj[1,2]. Better to construct bj in the transformed parameters block, which would require a bit of reorganization of the code, but would allow you to simply assign 0 to bj[1,2]. You’d do something like declare parameters:
> >
> > ordered[K-1] bj_raw[J-1];
> > real<upper=0> bj_init_a;
> > real<lower=0> bj_init_b;
> >
> > Then in the transformed parameters, declare vector[K-1] bj[J], and:
> >
> > bj[1,1]<-bj_init_a; bj[1,2]<-0; bj[1,3]<-bj_init_b;
> > for (j in 2:J) {
> > bj[j]<-bj_raw[j-1];
> > }
> >
> > and put the necessary priors on all the declared parameters (bj_raw, bj_init_a, bj_init_b).
> >
> > Hope that helps.
> >
> > Josh

> >> The model I'm working on (a version and simulated data are attached) is a graded response IRT model, where the difficulty parameter is decomposed into two components: an item component and a person component.  The person component would theoretically encompass response styles.  I am hoping to capture response style by having respondents answer items with regard to themselves, as well as a vignette (or three, in this case).  Response styles should remain constant across self-report, vignettes, and items.

The category cutpoints (bj) can be declared as ordered vectors, but the person parameters can't, so the sum of bi and bj is not always ordered.  The prior on bi_scale (uniform(0,3*N)) should keep bi in about the right range, given the distance between category cutpoints, but that doesn't seem to be enough.

Thank you for the advice - your code is much more elegant than my solution.

On Wednesday, July 23, 2014 4:58:22 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> On Jul 19, 2014, at 5:13 PM, Katherine Grace Jonas <katherine....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Is it possible to use logical statements to assign priors to a subset of elements in a matrix?
>
> Yes.  But it can be problematic if the conditions in the logical
> statements involve parameters, because it will usually introduce
> a discontinuity and hence non-differentiability of the resulting
> log posterior.
>
> >
> > In another thread, Josh suggested this solution, in order to fix location parameters in an IRT model:
> >
> > ordered[K-1] bj_raw[J-1];
> > real<upper=0> bj_init_a;
> > real<lower=0> bj_init_b;
> >
> > Then in the transformed parameters, declare vector[K-1] bj[J], and:
> >
> > bj[1,1]<-bj_init_a; bj[1,2]<-0; bj[1,3]<-bj_init_b;
> > for (j in 2:J) {
> > bj[j]<-bj_raw[j-1];
> > }
>
> Yes, this is one way to technically identify the location of an IRT model.
>
> >
> > If works well for a small matrix.  The priors can be assigned by:
> >
> > bj_init_1 ~ normal(0,1);
> >  bj_init_3 ~ normal(0,1);
> >  for (j in 1:(J-1)) {
> >  bj_raw[j] ~ normal(0,1);
> >  }
> >
> > What about a larger matrix, in which the fixed parameters are distributed more randomly?  Declaring, transforming, and sampling from a larger matrix might be prohibitively complicated.  Can it be done with logical statements?
>
> Yes, it can be done with logical statements.
>
> You can also go to a more database-like input to deal with ragged arrays.
> Something like:
>
>   int idx[K];
>   real param[K];
>
> Where param[k] is the parameter with index idx[k].
>
> > I have a matrix of parameters (para_raw), a matrix of transformed parameters (para_trans), and an indexing matrix (index), with 1s at positions to sample and 0s at the positions to fix.  The elements of para_trans are either fixed or transformed from para_raw in the transformed parameters block.  The code in the model block goes something like:
> >
> > for (r in 1:rows) {
> > for (c in 1:cols) {
> > if (index[r,c] != 0)
> > para_raw[r,c] ~ normal(0,1);
> > }
> > }
> >
> > The model runs, but samples for all elements of para_raw, not only the 1s.
>
> I'm not sure waht you mean by "the 1s".  You mean index[r,c] == 1?  You are
> putting a prior only on the para_raw[r,c] parameters for which
> index[r,c] != 0.
>
> All of the values in a transformed parameter will be printed out, but
> you will be able to see some that are fixed values (and thus have ill-defined
> R-hat values) and no variance in the posterior.
>
> > Is that because para_raw is declared as an r by c matrix?  Can STAN sample from only some elements of a declared variable, or does the variable need to be broken down into the elements to be estimated, as in Josh's code?  Is there some other way of accomplishing this?
>
> Yes, see above.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
You should be able to do just this:

  for (r in 1:R)

    orderedbla[r] <- sort_asc(bla[r]);

I worked hard to get row assignment working :-)

Now having said that, it's not efficient either way because
matrices are stored column-major.  So it's better if
you take an array of vectors:

  vector[C] bla[R];

or to make it more like a matrix, row vectors:

  row_vector[C] bla[R];

- Bob

Thanks for the pointer.

I wrote an initialization function in R that draws initial values from
my (weakly informative) priors, and then checks them for validity before
passing them to Stan. That seems to do the trick for the most part.

I still do get a few error messages from Stan in the early iterations
because something is over or underflowing and passing #IND values to
bernoulli_logit_log but once Stan has evaluated 100 or so samples, the
chains run with no further error messages, and looking at the traceplots
and density plots, it looks as though the chains mix nicely and don't
get stuck above or below 1, and with a few thousand samples, the
posterior density is smooth where it crosses 1 and Rhat for all the
parameters and lp__ are very close to 1.

Thanks for all the help and advice. Once I fixed the error Tamas pointed
out and got rid of the if statement, the stan computations sped up by a
couple of orders of magnitude (in effective samples per second).

Jonathan

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] automatic differentiation documentation
messages.body_plain:
There is no tutorial yet on how to use autodiff standalone.

What I would recommend is looking at src/stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp
to see if you can use the top-level functionals.  Those will autodiff
any functor with a vector argument.  The list of available functions
is pretty much what's documented in the Stan manual.

If that's not fine-grained enough control for you, I'd recommend
looking inside the implementations in autodiff.hpp, which provide
pretty simple examples of how to use the lower-level functionality.

There are also extensive unit tests in src/test/unit/agrad.

In Stan 2.4, the gradients are complete, but not the higher-order
autodiff.  They should be complete for 2.5.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Trouble with Multivariate Regression
messages.body_plain:
John,

I'm trying to implement precisely the model you described: multivariate data with t marginals and a normal copula. Have you implemented this model? Any advice on the best way to proceed?

I'm using a scale mixture representation, so each observation is augmented with a gamma distributed scaling parameter. I then construct the covariance matrix Sigma[t] for each time period, and sample using

y[t] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma[t])

(Everything is actually implemented in terms of Cholesky factors, and I sample using multi_normal_cholesky.) Overall, I'd say the results are pretty good for recovering the scale and location parameters, much less so for the degrees of freedom parameters -- even with a highly informative sample for which MLE works quickly and accurately.

Any thoughts or advice? Thanks.

Ravi

On Friday, January 24, 2014 9:46:03 AM UTC-6, John Hall wrote:
> Here are some references (the first is a more gentle introduction, the file is below the cached heading):
> http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.160.8266
> Nelson's "An Introduction to Copulas" is a popular reference that you could find at an academic library
> http://arxiv.org/abs/1112.4204
>
> Copulas are the multivariate dependence in a joint distribution. Sklar's theorem is the most important result, which says that any joint distribution can be expressed as some univariate distributions times the copula. The benefit of this approach is that you can model the univariate marginal distributions separately from the multivariate dependence. As such, copula estimation often requires the inverse pdf for the marginals, which might be one barrier to implementing them in Stan presently (I didn't see inverse pdfs in the manual).
>
> I used student t marginals and a normal copula as a good example above of why copulas are helpful. Basically, if you were to instead fit a multivariate student t distribution, then you effectively assume the degrees of freedom parameter is the same across every variable. The student t + normal copula would often be fit by first fitting each of the variables with a student t distribution with each having its own degrees of freedom. Then you would create a new multivariate variable applying the appropriate student t inverse pdf to each variable. This puts each variable between 0 and 1. To fit the normal copula to this, I might apply a standard normal cdf to that and estimate the resulting correlation matrix.

messages.subject: Re: hierarchical model with binary outcome
messages.subject_clean: hierarchical model with binary outcome
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joshua,

>From your code, I understand (and correct me if I'm wrong) that you are not using individual level predictors, right? If you are sticking to this intercept-only model, you could crank down significantly on computation by collapsing you data from (0/1) bernoulli responses to (k/N_kids) binomial responses, where N_kids is the number of children a mother had, and k is the number of kids that died. Then just model the binomial likelihood instead of the bernoulli:

for (i in 1:N_mothers)
    k[i] ~ binomial_logit(N_kids[i], intercept + int_4[ID4[i]] + int_3[ID3[i]] + int_2[ID2[i]] + int_1[ID1[i]]);

If on average mothers in your data have 2 kids, this means that you can compress your data (and number of likelihood evaluations) by a factor two. If at some point, you want to add individual-level predictors and these predictors are categorical (e.g. gender), you might to still apply aggregation, but now at the level of kid-gender | mother. Of course, if the number of kids per mother is low, this won't really have a significant impact.

Good luck,

Luc

messages.body_plain:
Ravi,
Just to give you a little more information. I think when I had first tried this, I didn't have much understanding of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. I still don't (compared to Gibbs Sampling), but I'm slightly more familiar with it than I used to be. The good thing about Gibbs sampling is that you can pretty much do whatever you want. Like I could throw in a PCA step to a Gibbs sampler and the only problem is that it slows everything down. You (likely) couldn't use PCA within the context of Stan because analytic formulas for PCA are ridiculous (I've tried symbolic math toolboxes for even 5x5 matrices and the formula look like just a sea of variables).

In Stan, you need to be able to provide analytic information for the log likelihood (or at least something proportional to it). The problem for a copula approach is that the copula log likelihood will have some quantile (inverse cdf) functions, depending on what the marginals are, that are not easy to calculate derivatives for. For instance, suppose you fit a t distribution to each univariate distribution. To fit the normal copula, you would then need to apply the cdf function for the relevant t to each univariate distribution and then apply the normal inverse cdf function to get normally distributed variables, which you could then estimate the correlation matrix from. Last time I checked, Stan has cdfs but not inverse cdfs, so at best you could get the uniform marginals (assuming Stan can handle taking derivatives of them, which I haven't tried). You'd then need some other approach to convert the uniform marginals to values, but even if you could write a user-defined function to do it (which you couldn't before) Stan would still need the derivatives of the functions for the HMC to work properly, I think at least.

messages.subject: Priors for constrained covariance matrices
messages.subject_clean: Priors for constrained covariance matrices
messages.body_plain:
In general multivariate modelling, the covariance matrix (say Sig) does not have any pattern or constrained (other than being positive-definite). So, Wishart kind of priors are used for Sig or Sig_inv. I have a model where the covariance matrix (or the Correlation matrix) has a pattern which induces some constrains on the correlation parameters (they are not free to be between -1 and +1). The constrains are higher order polynomials derived from forcing two determinants of sub-matrices to be positive. In WinBUGS the zero-trick is used to implement the constraints which does not always work. What is the alternative to the zero trick in rstan?

The correlation matrix is 4X4 matrix
1      phi1   phi2    phi3
phi1  1       phi3    phi2
phi2  phi3   1        phi4
phi3   phi2   phi4   1

Note that I have only four correlation parameters.
I have the analytical expressions for the inverse and determinants etc.  I can assign uniform(-1,1) priors for each of phi1, phi2, phi3 and phi4 BUT in addition have two constrains
det1 > 0 and det2 >0, where det1 and det2 are polynomials in phi's. I can't solve these polynomials to explicitly put constrains on individual phi's.

Has anyone encountered something like this? Such a model would arise in situations where the components of the Normal random variable have some kind of symmetry.

Paramjit

On Friday, August 15, 2014 2:26:00 AM UTC-4, Paramjit Gill wrote:
> I have a model where the covariance matrix (or the Correlation matrix) has a pattern which induces some constrains on the correlation parameters (they are not free to be between -1 and +1). The constrains are higher order polynomials derived from forcing two determinants of sub-matrices to be positive.

Nonlinear inequality constraints that are a function of multiple parameters are difficult to implement in Stan.

> In WinBUGS the zero-trick is used to implement the constraints which does not always work. What is the alternative to the zero trick in rstan?

Most likely you will have to declare an unrestricted correlation matrix and reject the proposal if either of the two submatrices have negative determinants. That may not work well in Stan either, depending on how much of the hypervolume of correlation matrices of order 4 are precluded by the constraints.

> The correlation matrix is 4X4 matrix
> 1      phi1   phi2    phi3
> phi1  1       phi3    phi2
> phi2  phi3   1        phi4
> phi3   phi2   phi4   1
>
> Note that I have only four correlation parameters.
> I have the analytical expressions for the inverse and determinants etc.  I can assign uniform(-1,1) priors for each of phi1, phi2, phi3 and phi4 BUT in addition have two constrains
> det1 > 0 and det2 >0, where det1 and det2 are polynomials in phi's. I can't solve these polynomials to explicitly put constrains on individual phi's.

What are these polynomials? It is possible that you could declare in the parameters block

parameters {
  real<lower=-1,upper=1> phi1;
  real<lower=something,upper=else> phi2; # depending on realization of phi1
  real<lower=something,upper=else> phi3; # depending on realization of phi1 and phi2
  real<lower=something,upper=else> phi4; # depending on realization of phi1, phi2, and phi3
}

where something and else depend on lower-order polynomials.

> Has anyone encountered something like this? Such a model would arise in situations where the components of the Normal random variable have some kind of symmetry.

I can imagine, but I don't think I have seen anything like that in the literature.

Ben

eyeballing the model, it turned out it was misspecified (one variable
which ostensibly had a lognormal distribution assumed a 0 value for some
of the data).

statements of left- and right hand sides. I was wondering if there is a
quicker way of doing this, so I thought I would print lp__ before and
after each statement and then I would notice if it gets to a nonsensical
value.

However, it always printed the same (!) value for me, and stan of course
warned me that lp__ is deprecated (I am using 2.4). So I am wondering
how to do what I originally wanted the "right" way --- is there a way to
print the lp__ increment for each sampling statement?

Best,

Tamas

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] [Cmd/Py/R-Stan] how to debug vanishing density?
messages.body_plain:
D'oh!  It just dawned on me what the problem is.  For efficiency,
the log prob increment statements add to an accumulator and then
apply sum() at the end, rather than incrementing lp__ directly.
The increment is only at the very end, after all the model statements
get called.  Until then, you're seeing only the Jacobian from constrained
variables all the way through.

I'm going to add a log_prob() function with no-args ASAP
that will go through the accumulator and print the sum.  Then that
will be the recommended function for debugging lp():

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/470

The other thing we need to do is not swallow the warning messages.
Right now, initialization swallows the warning message then tries again.
Those should print.   I re-opened the issue which had been prematurely
closed (or perhaps it moved --- I can't find the new target, so I reopened
this one):

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/779

The big goal, which isn't going to happen right away, is to get
line numbers into the error reports.  We know how to do it, but it's
going to be a fair bit of work.

I'll get the first one done for Stan 2.5 and the second done for
CmdStan, but then the same behavior needs to be replicated in PyStan
and RStan.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
There's a discussion on the dev list that sounds a lot like a problem I complained about but never had the time to solve.
The discussion implicates R's internal RecursiveRelease (as triggered by RStan), which sometimes causes a stack overflow.

There's a thread from r-devel that links this type of problem (with an example that triggers a stack overflow) to use of R's
protect/unprotect macros.

Link to R list: https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-devel/2010-January/056257.html
Link to Stan list: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/BujPDKpUDp0/8chCkyn5wQAJ

It sounds like there was talk of a patch but I don't know if it ever happened.

Krzysztof

Overflow stats not available

- PROTECT/UNPROTECT get used directly in RStan (not sure why since there are Rcpp-level interfaces for the same thing but ok) and
- PROTECT/UNPROTECT get used indirectly in RStan via Rcpp wrappers for R objects

My pet issue (https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/76) triggers a stack overflow after a long time and I figured out it was _some_ sort

You mentioned (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/BujPDKpUDp0/1a_1yOjI8vc) you
can also get a stack overflow on a simple model as well and an otherwise mysterious performance problem with large data.
In the (linked) post from R-devel, one of the posters (Romain Francois) shows that with the current RecursiveRelease implementation
you get a stack overflow if the thing to release is far enough down a list of objects.  His code is at:

https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-devel/attachments/20100103/2f8abd90/attachment.pl

It looks like he used the R API for this, but I'm not sure if he exactly replicates RecursiveRelease.

A bit from the R-devel list about PROTECT/UNPROTECT, RecursiveRelease, stack usage,

----------------------
>>>> PROTECT/UNPROTECT is trading granularity for speed. It is a stack with
>>>> only tow operations possible:
>>>> - push 1 object into the stack
>>>> - pull (unprotect) N last objects from the stack
>>>>
>>> UNPROTECT_PTR is also possible, which does a linear search through the
>>> stack and unprotects something possibly deep within it. There is also
>>> REPROTECT which allows you to replace an entry within the stack.
>>>
>>> I would guess that UNPROTECT_PTR is more efficient than RecursiveRelease
>>> because it doesn't use so much stack space when it needs to go deep into
>>> the stack to release, but it is possible the compiler recognizes the
>>> tail recursion and RecursiveRelease is implemented efficiently. In that
>>> case it could be more efficient than UNPROTECT_PTR, which has to move
>>> all the other entries down to fill the newly vacated space. Really the
>>> only reliable way to answer efficiency questions like this is to try
>>> both ways and see which works better in your application.
>>>
>> Thanks. I did not know about UNPROTECT_PTR.
>> I had concerns over the stack usage, but so far it did not prove too much of a problem.
>> Still, why isn't the tail recursion explicitly made an iteration then ? This would take
>> the "may be the compiler figures it out, may be not" variable out of the equation.
>>
>>
>
> Careful - the protection stack (bookkeeping by R) has nothing to do with the C function call stack hence it has nothing to do with the compiler. The protection stack is global so usually you don't run out of it unless something goes horribly wrong (=infinite loop).
>

I think Laurent was referring to RecursiveRelease, which could use a lot
of C stack if you choose to release something that is deep in the list,
since it checks the head, and if that doesn't match, calls itself again
on the rest of the list.  (I checked, and at least one version of gcc
doesn't recognize the tail recursion:  it really does generate a
recursive call.)

Laurent asked why it isn't optimized to avoid the recursion:  I think
the answer is simply because it is so rarely used that nobody has bothered.
----------------------end R-devel

So my guess is that Rstan when it goes to execute the model (rstan::(anonymous namespace)::execute_sampling<model3cc11....)
It triggers RecursiveRelease to be called and we get the slow down and/or stack overflow.  ... I don't know if there's an explicit copying of temporaries somewhere
that does this or if it's some mysterious part of R's GC but I think your profiling and the R-devel discussion narrows it down a little more.

Krzysztof

> Ben

Thank you all for your time and help!

Ravi

messages.subject: suggestions for enhancing print
messages.subject_clean: suggestions for enhancing print
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have been doing a lot of debugging by printf lately. Since this is the
only practical way to debug models that I know of, I think that making
it a bit more convenient (= less typing) would be a huge
improvement. The two proposals below reflect the way I usually debug
code, which may not be universal, but still this could be a starting
point for a discussion (I checked the issues and could not find anything
similar, sorry if I missed something).

1. Printing arguments to the print call

Instead of writing

print("i = ", i, ", x[i] = ", x[i], ", y[i] = ", y[i]);

there could be a function printvars which would be called as

printvars(i, x[i], y[i]);

This would print its arguments, too, followed by values, separated by
commas. In Lisp-like languages one would implement printvars as a macro,
since it needs to see the variable names it was called with, and I don't
know if the parser of Stan retains this information.

When printvars encounters a literal string, it could just print that as
is, eg

printvars("debugging inner loop", i, x[i], y[i]);

would be equivalent to

print("debugging inner loop", "i = ", i, ", x[i] = ", x[i], ", y[i] = ", y[i]);

2. Interpolating, similar to printf. I guess there is no need to
explain. Would extend current print in an upward-compatible way (except
if one uses % in strings).

3. Interpolating version of printvars: literal strings that have
formatting directives would just gobble as many of the following
arguments as needed, but otherwise it would work as printvars.

(2) and (3) are wishlist items, I understand that the Stan developers
are busy with a lot of other things, but just plain vanilla printvars
(1) would make debugging a lot easier.

Best,

Tamas

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would like to ask for some help in formulating the following model in
Stan.

I have N individuals, indexed with i=1, ..., N. I have two _latent_
variables w and z, constrained to be > 0, so I would initially start my
analysis with lognormal, eg

for (i in 1:N) {
  w[i] ~ lognormal(mu_w, sigma_w);
  z[i] ~ lognormal(mu_z, sigma_z);
}

So far, nothing is observable. The two observables y and n have the
following data generating process: there is a parameter m > 0, and when

z[i]/w[i] > m, n[i]=0 and y[i]=0;

otherwise n[i] is a linear function of z[i]/w[i] and y[i] is a linear
function of z[i] and w[i] (I need the coefficients, and I can always add
a lognormal error etc).

My problem is with the part when z[i]/w[i] > m. It is clear that I need
to separate the observations into two groups, one where n[i]=y[i]=0, the
other is when it isn't.

But I don't know how to tell Stan that in the first group, observations
for which z/w < m have a 0 likelihood --- should I somehow set lp__ to
minus infinity conditional on this happening?

Best,

Tamas

Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> writes:

> On Wednesday, August 13, 2014 1:38:21 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>> The downside is that with more doc, it's much harder to
>> keep in synch (takes more time, inconsistencies more likely).
>>
>
> I don't know how you make your docs (plain LaTeX?) but at least with knitr
> (which will mix LaTeX with R/Python and other languages) it's possible to
> include outside
> scripts as chunks of code.  That might take care of inconsistencies.

Org-mode under Emacs does that, too.

I see in a separate note that you use LaTeX.  One tool that might have
advantages is DocBook (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DocBook).  It is
designed to make it easier to pull together pre-defined chunks that you
reuse in various documents -- "Write once, read anywhere."

For example, you write the chunks that you need for various documents,
and you assemble the pieces you need from those chunks for each document
you want.  You can, at least to a significant degree, use the equivalent
of variables in text, so that you could have one document for generic
Stan and plug in CmdStan, RStan, PyStan, or any other Stan as
appropriate to the document you're generating.

Then you process the document to produce a PDF manual, an online Web
page, or whatever you need.  I tend to use the route through dblatex to
create PDFs, so that turns the DocBook source into LaTeX on its way to
PDF.

As DocBook source is XML and XML can be wordy, you may want help in
creating it.  I've used Emacs' nxml-mode and found it good.  I'm told
there are GUI approaches (perhaps in LibreOffice).

DITA is a similar, alternative approach I've read about but never used.

Of course, perhaps LaTeX is exactly what you want.

Bill

messages.body_plain:
If you set the log probability to -infinity, it will do rejection.
It's better to actually implement the constraints.  The problem is
that Stan doesn't let you separately implement constraints for
each variable.

So you have to enforce this constraint yourself:

> z[i]/w[i] > m

Rewriting, that's

  z[i] > m / w[i]

So you need a lower-bound on z[i] equal to m / w[i].

The way to do this is just do what Stan does internally for
transformed parameters.  Start with a raw, unconstrained parameter,
then transform it and apply the Jacobian adjustment:

parameters {
  vector[N] z_raw;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] z;

  for (i in 1:N)

    z[i] <- exp(z_raw) + m / w[i];
  increment_log_prob(z_raw);  // adds complete Jacobian
}
model {
   z ~ ...; // whatever prior you want here
}

Here's the relevant log Jacobian calculation:

     log abs( d/dz_raw exp(z_raw) )
      = log abs(exp(z_raw))
      = z_raw

You can make the whole thing explicit in a big Jacobian
matrix which has identity transforms for m and w.

Then you can put whatever prior on z you want.

- Bob

On Aug 15, 2014, at 11:52 PM, Ravi Sastry <ravis...@gmail.com> wrote:

> John and Luc,
>
> I was (of course) hoping to let Stan generate the full joint log density and gradient on its own. But if my current approach doesn't work out, and since there is no support yet for copula distributions, I will need to explicitly specify the log density as you suggest. Those approximations for erf() may prove essential.
>
> Herra,
>
> I'll make the change to my declared bounds to see if it fixes things. I hope so! But my simpler model with univariate t data using the scale mixture representation had the same bounds and priors on the relevant parameters, and that converged without issue. Do you know if the Stan documentation warns against specifying a prior whose support doesn't exactly match the declared bounds?

> (As you see from my code, I assumed that having prior support a subset of the declared bounds would be OK.)

You can only do it the other way around.

For instance, a half-Cauchy prior can be defined by

  parameters {
    real<lower=0> sigma;
    ...
  }
  model
    sigma ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
    ...

You only need an explicit truncation when either one of the bounds or
one of the parameters of the distribution is a parameter --- otherwise, you
can just drop it, as above, where it would be T[0,].

But if you do this:

  parameters {
    real sigma;
    ...
  }
  model {
    sigma ~ lognormal(0,1);
    ...

you'll almost certainly run into problems sampling when sigma goes below 0
either doing initialization or during the Hamiltonian dynamics.  That causes
a rejection, and if it's an init, that's fatal.

- Bob

Hi Bob,

I tried something like you suggested on simulated data, and everything
works out except for the truncation parameter. In particular, my data
generating process is

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
N <- 10000
z <- rlnorm(N)
w <- rlnorm(N)
d <- data.frame(z=z, w=w)
d[, "z_hat"] <- d$z * rlnorm(N, 0, 0.1)
d[, "w_hat"] <- d$w * rlnorm(N, 0, 0.1)
d <- d[d$z/d$w > 1, ]                   # m=1
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

ie z, w are unit lognormal, only a noisy version z_hat, w_hat is
observed, data is kept iff z/w >  m = 1.

And the corresponding stan model is

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real<lower=0> z_hat[N];
  real<lower=0> w_hat[N];
}

parameters {
  real w_aux[N];
  real z_aux[N];
  real m_aux;
}

transformed parameters {
  real m;
  real w[N];
  real z[N];
  m <- exp(m_aux);

  for (i in 1:N) {

    w[i] <- exp(w_aux[i]);
    z[i] <- exp(z_aux[i]) + m*w[i];
  }
}

model {
  increment_log_prob(m_aux);

  for (i in 1:N) {

    z[i] ~ lognormal(0.0, 1.0);
    w[i] ~ lognormal(0.0, 1.0);
    z_hat[i]/z[i] ~ lognormal(0, 0.1);
    w_hat[i]/w[i] ~ lognormal(0, 0.1);
    increment_log_prob(z_aux[i]);
    increment_log_prob(w_aux[i]);
  }
}
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

I run and check it with

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
model <- stan_model(file = "bivariate_censoring1.stan")
fit <- sampling(model,
                data =
                  list(N = nrow(d),
                       z_hat = d$z_hat,
                       w_hat = d$w_hat),
                iter=1000,
                chains=1)
posterior <- extract(fit, permuted = TRUE)
plot(d$z, colMeans(posterior$z))
abline(a=0, b=1, col="gray50")
plot(d$w, colMeans(posterior$w))
abline(a=0, b=1, col="gray50")
hist(posterior$m)
abline(v=1, col="gray50")
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

and everything checks out except that the posterior mean of m is well
below 1, and also, it depends on the sample size. I know that censoring
boundaries are tricky to identify well, but I am still wondering if I
miscoded something.

Also, I get a couple of
--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::lognormal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Random variable is -nan:0, but must not be nan!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---
messages but not more than 1-2 per chain, so I think these can be
ignored safely.

Best,

Tamas

> If you don’t want to read my code I will explain again my problem literally:
>
> Suppose you have 10 (two times 3 position- and 2 polarangle-parameters). They need to be transformed, because each position-prior has individual borders. Each position-parameter is transformed, meaning you get for each parameter one and just one transformed parameter! This means you would get a quadratic Jacobi-Matrix and you could calculate the determinant. In this case I don’t need to add the determinant of the Jacobi to the Log-Probability-function, because it is a linear transformation and it is only necessary to determine the Log-Probability-function up to constant in Stan.

You lost me here.  I think you will need a Jacobian because of the
non-linear transforms going into fret_eff.  But you should really
decide whether the model you mean is

  fret_avg[i] ~ normal(fret_eff, fret_err[i]);

Also, you want to vectorize, so that'd be:

  fret_eff ~ normal(fret_avg, fret_err);

> Further the polarangle-parameters are changed to express the same vectors in Cartesian coordinates. Because these vectors have by definition the length one, only two parameters  (theta and phi) are transformed to three parameters moment[j,1], moment[j,2] and moment[j,3]. This means we need to construct a Jacobi-Matrix that is of type 3x2. Here the calculation of a determinant isn’t as trivial as above. Do we need then the generalized functional determinant (therefore the square of the gramian determinant) for ?

>
>
>
> Now suppose we want to calculate the Log-Probability-function, but the function is so complex, that it is easier and better readable to calculate it from inside to outside. This is what happens in the model block in the above example.
>
> The local variable fret_eff, which is normal distributed and defines the Log-Probability-function, depends on the distance (dist) between two positions (position-parameters) and on the so called averaged Förster Radius (R_avg), which is defined by various angles (cThX) between two moments (vector[3] moment) and the linking vector of two positions. This means I calculate at first the linking vector out of the two position vectors, its length as the distance and then the above mentioned various angles. The latter are used to calculate R_avg and finally we can define the sampling statement, which states that fret_eff is sampled from a normal distribution with variance and mean defined in the data block.
>
> So from my understanding we need to adjust the Log-Probability-function with the Jacobi-determinant of the transformation, if we have a “Change of variables”, which means that the transformed parameters are sampled instead of the parameters! If this is correct, does it mean, that I have to build a huge Jacobi-Matrix from the variable fret_eff derived by all untransformed parameters (what would lead to an unsymmetric matrix, more exact to a row-vector) and calculate its gramian determinant to account for the curvature of the transformation?

Yes.  But I have no idea how to do that.

> To make my problem as clear as possible, here again in an example free way:
>

> Is it allowed to split your function in several steps (outside of a sampling statement) and just sample the result of these split steps. If not, what is the correct way to handles this? If it is, are those steps considered as transformations? If they are considered as transformations (and we are dealing with “Change of variables”) how do you compute the determinant of an unsymmetric matrix (by gramian matrix?) in case of variable reduction during transformation?

To sum up, you are going to need to work this out yourself (or with
help from someone other than me!) what you want the posterior density
to be.  Then you have to code that in Stan.

Stan will automatically apply Jacobians implied by any constraints
on variables.  The rest are up to you if you use transformed parameters
on the left of sampling statements.

- Bob

Thanks for your effort!

the true value (using simulated data) --- in fact, the region does not

m <- 1 # boundary

is m, here = 1, but the stan model (at the link above) estimates it far
below that, moreover, the distribution is not really consistent across
runs (with 1000 iterations).

While it is most likely that I am facing a conceptual issue that I need
to understand, I wonder if I ran into a bug.

Best,

Tamas

messages.subject_clean: censoring model misfit (minimal example)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tamar,

I think you can only estimate parameter m if you know what the scale of the noise in z_hat is. If you are trying to estimate both the scale of the noise and threshold m, the posterior will entirely depend on what priors you use.

The problem is that the simulated data hold no information on the relative contributions of the noise and the threshold to the marginal variance of the data, unless you have repeated observation of z_hat[ij] | z[j] (which will provide information about the scale of the noise). From your data simulation, it seems you have no repeated observations of z_hat[ij] | z[j], though.

Maybe I'm wrong, but you might want to test it by actually setting the noise term in your model to same value as your data-generating process, or simulate repeated observations z_hat[ij]. Then, threshold m should be identifiable.

Best,

Luc

messages.body_plain:
Sorry, I spoke/wrote too soon. Should have read your model code more carefully.

The discrepancy may actually be due to the fact that your are assuming different distributions for z in the data-generating process and in the model. You use left-truncated log-normal for data generation, whereas you assume that z = m + exp(z_aux), where z_aux follows an improper uniform prior. I'm not sure those two things are the same. Why not model z directly as z ~ lognormal(0,1) [m,]; ?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This is a simplified example from a bivariate censoring problem which
does not admit such a simple formulation, hence the need to model it
this way (see [1]. For the univariate case I could, of course, use
Stan's truncated distros, but the original problem came up for a more
complicated model and I want to keep things similar.

In any case, z_aux has an improper/flat \propto 1 prior, which means
that it does not contribute to the posterior, so it is harmless. I have
a prior on z anyway.

Best,

Tamas

[1] https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/PZE0tkwJ2A4

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Loss of parameters in output file
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Loss of parameters in output file
messages.body_plain:
On Aug 19, 2014, at 3:53 AM, Tobias Eilert <tobias.e...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hey Bob,
>
> the problem is not that I just WANT to sample from a transformed parameter, but I HAVE to:
> First of all in each sampling scenario the number of position-priors differs, that means I need an array with flexible size!

Stan doesn't have a ragged array data type, so the only way to
deal with this is with the ugly encoding demonstrated for LDA
in the manual.

> Further each position-prior has individual prior-borders (also changing in different scenarios), but in Stan you can not create an array where each field has different borders!

Correct.

> So I have to create an array, where each field is bordered from 0 to 1 and transform them with the individual borders read in the data block.

Correct.  It doesn't matter where you start (other than for
efficiency) as long as you apply all the Jacobians necessary.

> Because for the calculation of fret_eff the distance between the transformed position-priors is needed I can not sample from the first array of untransformed parameters!
>
> Second of all the Log-Probability-function, if I write it directly depending on the transformed parameters (and not split into steps), is more than ugly and almost impossible to debug!

We don't have a solution for that.

> If you want a Stan-Code that reproduces in cmdStan the loss of parameters take one of those I've posted in my opening mail (e.g. FRETnps_seq.stan with data sheet FRETnps_data.data.R). Yesterday evening one possible reason came to my mind: I opened the data sheet with Excel. Maybe Excel is the problem...

Thanks.

> Why should I want to sample fret_avg (= expectation of the fret_eff) which I get from the input?

It's a different model.  In a linear regression, you get y from the input
with coefficients beta and predictors beta, but you model it using a sampling statement.

  y ~ normal(X * beta, sigma);

The normal is symmetric in the first two arguments, so technically this is the
same log probability increment:

  X * beta ~ normal(y, sigma);

> You're right with the vectorization! But before I think about the implementation I want to be sure that my code samples the correct posterior!!!

Good idea.

- Bob
